#644. Breaking: Not Worcestershire: Make Steak 10x More Tender With This Saucy Condiment

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (552 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic

Breaking: Not Worcestershire: Make Steak 10x More Tender With This Saucy Condiment

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that whether it's Worcestershire sauce or a freshly brewed cup of coffee, there are plenty of creative marinades that'll give your steak a super tender texture.
  • Originating in Thailand, sriracha is a hugely popular tangy, garlicky chili sauce made from a blend of chili peppers, garlic, vinegar, sugar, and salt, and is best known in the U.S.
  • In a recent development, because the marinade is acidic, it only needs 30 minutes to a few hours in the fridge to get to work, and overly long soaks are best avoided, as they can leave the outside of the meat mushy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that whether it's Worcestershire sauce or a freshly brewed cup of coffee, there are plenty of creative marinades that'll give your steak a super tender texture. What unites all these hacks is one secret component: acidity. Another pantry essential loaded with it that will bring some delicious Asian-inspired flair to your next steak is sriracha.

Originating in Thailand, sriracha is a hugely popular tangy, garlicky chili sauce made from a blend of chili peppers, garlic, vinegar, sugar, and salt, and is best known in the U.S. for the iconic rooster-labeled bottle from Huy Fong Foods. Sriracha can help tenderize meat because of its vinegar content, with the acetic acid helping break down proteins on the surface of the meat. This marinade can be particularly useful with tougher cuts like flank or round steak. These cuts are often cheaper than well-marbled ones like ribeye or Newly introduced York strip, but that comes at the cost of natural tenderness.

In a recent development, because the marinade is acidic, it only needs 30 minutes to a few hours in the fridge to get to work, and overly long soaks are best avoided, as they can leave the outside of the meat mushy. Sriracha has a naturally thick, ketchup-like consistency, so it helps to thin it with a splash of liquid like soy sauce, lime juice, or even oil, which turns it into a pourable marinade that coats every inch of the surface. For even coverage, toss the steak in a zip-top bag and leave it there to marinate. To tenderize tougher cuts even further, slice the steak thinly against the grain after cooking, which shortens the muscle fibers for an easier, more satisfying bite.

It has been revealed that A marinade is more than a hodgepodge of ingredients. It's a balanced blend that works to boost the flavor and texture of your steak, and the building blocks of a great one are salt, acid, oil, and seasonings. Sriracha stands out, as it already has three of these four components covered. We've already covered the acid, but sriracha is also high in salt, one of its five main ingredients. Alongside the vinegar, salt helps tenderize the meat by drawing out moisture through osmosis, which dissolves the salt into a brine that's then reabsorbed. This absorbed salt adds a deeper flavor, helps the meat retain moisture, and alters muscle proteins for a juicier, tastier steak.

But tenderizing the surface is only half the job, since you've also got to cover flavor. Here, the chili and garlic get to work, adding depth and a little heat to the steak. If you really want an extra mouthwatering result, look for a sriracha that contains MSG, which is specifically used to bring umami to dishes, alongside the core ingredients.

The one missing element sriracha hasn't got covered is oil, but this is a quick and easy fix. Simply mix it with a high-smoke-point oil — think canola, vegetable, or avocado oil, Bobby Flay's favorite oil for cooking up a ribeye. Many of the flavor compounds found in sriracha, like those in garlic and chili, are fat-soluble. When you stir them into oil, the oil helps extract and distribute these flavors evenly over the surface of the meat, helping deepen and intensify its flavor.

It has been revealed that I wouldn't call myself a minimalist by any means, but I am not someone who buys a lot of kitchen gadgets or rushes to snag the latest seasonal cup. But ever since I picked up my first Fellow Carter Move Mug five years ago, I’ve happily repurchased it several times.

This sleek little mug, designed by the coffee nerds at Fellow, keeps your brew hot (or cold) without sacrificing flavor. I use it so often that I’ve sung its praises to a coffee shop owner in Washington, a bed-and-breakfast proprietor in Maine, and countless other strangers.

I love this mug more than I can express—so much, in fact, that I reached out to Fellow founder, Jake Miller, to chat about it. Miller stated this effective temperature control is from two things: the distance between the two walls and how much vacuum insulation the mug has. Also, Fellow designed the lid to be gasket-tight so there’s minimal heat loss.

Industry observers note that one of my favorite features of the Move Mug is the splash guard that clicks into the vessel and prevents big spills while you’re drinking in motion. This element, along with some other accessories, was born out of feedback based on how customers use their mugs, including a straw for cold coffee, a cup holder-friendly size, and the option for a slide top lid. “Everything we do is customer-driven,” Miller noted.

In a recent development, maybe not important to how your coffee tastes — but important to aesthetics — the Move Mug is sleek and sophisticated, which means it’s suitable for most situations. There’s a nice range of colors, and it looks great in my hand on my commute and on my desk in the office. It’s truly the perfect accessory.

#642. 6 Once-Popular Buffet Chains That Went Extinct

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1428 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic

6 Once-Popular Buffet Chains That Went Extinct

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1428 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • All-you-can-eat buffets were once a common feature in the restaurant world.
  • Sources indicate that there are still a few all-you-can-eat buffets around.
  • Souplantation, which was called Sweet Tomatoes outside of its home state of California, was a self-service buffet that operated over 120 locations in the mid-2010s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

All-you-can-eat buffets were once a common feature in the restaurant world. Now-defunct chains like Shoney's, Fire Mountain, and Luby's were popular because the businesses offered endless plates of a wide variety of foods for a set price. This allowed customers to try fresh things and enjoy familiar items without having to order separate dishes and paying more. The concept was so popular even fast food chains, like Popeyes, had buffets. But the format is becoming a rarity these days, partially due to rising food and labor costs.

Sources indicate that there are still a few all-you-can-eat buffets around. For instance, seafood buffets are popular on the East Coast, as well as in Las Vegas. And mega-retailer Walmart was able to help revive the failing Mr. Gatti's Pizza, which was once known for it's oversized buffets. But today, the pizza restaurant is much smaller and operates a more traditional order-and-take-out model. Not every chain was as lucky as Mr. Gatti's, and that's why this list highlights some of the reasons once-popular buffet chains don't exist anymore.

Souplantation, which was called Sweet Tomatoes outside of its home state of California, was a self-service buffet that operated over 120 locations in the mid-2010s. The restaurant first opened in 1978 and was known for its large selection of soups and fresh muffins. Even though the chain was popular, it began to falter as the minimum wage and rent prices increased. These combined factors led to the company filing for bankruptcy in 2016.

The business was already on shaky ground when the COVID-19 pandemic hit in 2020. Because of the uncertain nature of the disease early in the shutdown, self-service wasn't allowed in restaurants. Souplantation couldn't last without customers any more than it could suddenly become a full-service eatery. So, in May 2020, the last 97 locations were permanently shut down.

But that wasn't the end for the brand, because there are now two re-opened Sweet Tomatoes restaurants. One is in Arizona, and the other is in Florida. That might make the tech giant more of a novelty for now than a comeback success story, with a third location set to open in California in 2027, there's no telling what lies ahead for the brand.

Old Country Buffet was one of the largest buffet chains in the country, with nearly 400 stores during the early 2000s. It was known for its selection of over 90 items that were made from scratch each day. It was so popular it was able to grow to 200 locations in just a decade and rivaled Outback Steakhouse in sales. This beloved buffet closed during the COVID-19 pandemic, but financial complications had plagued the business long before.

According to recent reports, it began in 2006, when the brand's parent tech giant, Buffets, Inc., merged with Ryan's. The move gave the company more buffet concepts and locations, but it also brought massive debt. That caused the business to file for bankruptcy protection in 2008 and again in 2012. Old Country Buffet's parent company was bought by Ovation Brands Inc. (also called Buffets LLC) in 2015, but the fresh owners shuttered almost 100 stores early the next year.

According to recent reports, there was another bankruptcy in 2016, which further weakened the brand. When the COVID-19 pandemic hit a few years later, the loss of its remaining customers sealed the chain's fate. A final Chapter 11 protection was filed in 2021, which closed the remaining stores.

Sources indicate that homeTown Buffet was never as widespread as its sister restaurants, Old Country Buffet and Ryan's, but at its height there were over 120 locations throughout the U.S. The company was started in 1989 and, as the name implies, was dedicated to home-style cooking and comforting foods. The brand became part of Buffets, Inc. in the mid-1990s. But not long after, HomeTown Buffet's parent company began having legal and financial troubles due to alleged fraud and multiple bankruptcies.

The first bankruptcy happened in 2008, and it did help reduce some of the debt the company had. But it wasn't enough to keep the business going. So, other bankruptcies were filed in 2012 and 2016. More than 70 locations were closed with the Chapter 11 protection in 2016, which was over half of the brand's stores.

Sources indicate that there were legal issues, too, with a 2010 lawsuit alleging several of the parent company's executives had used nearly $40 million as their personal funds. In 2015, the brand settled a class action filing alleging it hadn't paid workers their final wages for around $2 million. There was even an investigation by the State of California in 2016 over whether the company had illegally laid off workers without the required warnings. In the end, all of the problems HomeTown Buffet had led to one final bankruptcy filing in 2021, which closed all the remaining locations.

Those who were lucky enough to eat at a Ryan's Buffet when the chain was open are likely to remember the famous yeast rolls. The bread and honey butter it was served with were key parts of this buffet experience at any of the restaurant's over 350 locations during its height. But the business was also owned by the parent company of HomeTown and Old Country Buffets, so Ryan's suffered from the same financial mismanagement and legal troubles the other businesses did.

The concerns started in 2006 when Buffets, Inc. wanted to buy Ryan's. Shareholders at the time were unhappy the organization had been put up for sale without full transparency, so they filed a lawsuit to stop the sale. Ryan's settled with the shareholders and went ahead with the merger. But that led to large amounts of debt.

According to recent reports, in 2008 and 2012, the tech giant began filing bankruptcies, which led to a domino effect of locations closing, beginning in 2016. The COVID-19 pandemic didn't help the business any more than its parent company being accused of mishandling over $4 million in Paycheck Protection Program funds did. One final bankruptcy finished off the chain in 2021.

Founded in Pensacola, Florida in 1991, Barnhill's Buffet was known for Southern-style food that the founder, Steve Barnhill, was proud to say was better seasoned than other all-you-can-eat options. That superior taste helped expand the brand to over 40 locations across six states by 2005. However, the food alone couldn't keep the doors open.

Sources indicate that several locations in Southern Mississippi were heavily damaged by Hurricane Katrina in 2005, causing them to close. That was just the start of Barnhill's financial troubles. The tech giant filed for bankruptcy in December 2007, while nearly $28 million in debt. Sixteen stores were sold to Star Buffet Management Inc. in 2008, but just a few years later multiple locations were shuttered. Barnhill's had just one location left after closing the rest in the early 2000s. The Jonesboro, Arkansas store held on until 2021 but was forced to close due to owing a substantial amount in back rent.

While that was the end of the original brand, Steve Barnhill created another restaurant bearing his name called Barnhill's Steaks & Buffet. This stand-alone eatery is found in Jacksonville, Arkansas, and even though it isn't as cheap as the very first all-you-can-eat buffet, the prices are shockingly low.

According to recent reports, whether you knew it as Furr's Cafeteria or Furr's Fresh Buffet, this business was a powerhouse of cafeteria and buffet-style dining from its founding in the 1940s until it was shuttered in early 2021. The all-you-can-eat concept boasted nine buffet stations for everything from ice cream to salads to a variety of proteins and operated in five different states. But things weren't going smoothly for the brand after it reformatted its cafeteria locations into buffets.

As early as 2008, Furr's was having financial troubles and was reportedly more than $40 million in debt. An ice storm in 2013 further weakened the business when numerous customers in Texas and Oklahoma weren't able to dine out, leading the manufacturer to declare its third bankruptcy in 2014. Locations began closing, with one Midland, Texas store going out of business in 2018.

According to recent reports, just a few years later, the chain's parent firm, Fresh Acquisitions LLC, declared bankruptcy again, after it was accused of mishandling millions of dollars of Paycheck Protection Program loans. That led to every remaining Furr's location being shut down in 2021. But unlike other buffets that have been forgotten, Furr's still has fans who recreate the brand's dishes through food trucks and special themed restaurant nights.

Industry News: Ferrero Rocher Blossom Cookies

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (207 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that in a separate bowl, whisk together the flour, cocoa powder and salt.
  • In a small bowl, whisk the egg white until it’s foamy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Industry observers note that in a large bowl, cream the butter and sugar with a handheld mixer until they’re light and fluffy, five to seven minutes. Beat in the egg yolk, milk and vanilla.

Sources indicate that in a separate bowl, whisk together the flour, cocoa powder and salt. Gradually add the dry ingredients to the creamed mixture, mixing until a soft dough forms. Cover and refrigerate the dough for about one hour, or until it’s firm enough to handle.

Preheat the oven to 350°F. In a small bowl, whisk the egg white until it’s foamy. Shape the chilled dough into 1-1/2-inch balls. Dip the balls into the egg white, letting any excess drip off, then roll them in the chopped hazelnuts to coat.

Editor’s Tip: A piping bag or small zip-top bag with one corner snipped off makes it easy to add the Nutella neatly to the centers.

If the dough starts to feel sticky when you’re shaping it, pop it back in the refrigerator for another 15 to 20 minutes. You want it firm enough to handle without sticking to your fingers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve had quite a few dreams and aspirations in my adult life thus far.
  • Recent findings suggest that besides the obvious barriers to entry of price and counter space, one of the main reasons I waited so long to make my dream a reality was that, well, I was intimidated.
  • That’s why, when I got wind a couple years ago that Breville was launching a latest top of the line, not-quite automatic espresso machine that promised to guide me through all of the processes I was intimidated by, I was immediately intrigued.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve had quite a few dreams and aspirations in my adult life thus far. One of them was owning an espresso machine. As someone who would typically choose a cappuccino over a cup of drip coffee, the idea of waking up every morning and enjoying the perfect mug of milky espresso from the comfort of my own home seemed like the pinnacle of luxury.

Recent findings suggest that besides the obvious barriers to entry of price and counter space, one of the main reasons I waited so long to make my dream a reality was that, well, I was intimidated. The world of coffee—and espresso in particular—is one that intrigues me, but I’m admittedly no expert. And while the science nerd in me feels somewhat compelled to spend time delving deep into grind size and ratios and extraction times, the reality is I’ve always felt daunted at the prospect of actually doing so—and wary of investing in a machine that would be so complicated to use, I’d end up forgoing it anyway. At the same time, I shied away from the idea of fully automatic machines that operate at the push of a button, because the wannabe barista in me wants to feel like I’m doing something as I make my morning cup. That, and I’ve never found the espresso those kinds of machines make to be all that good.

That’s why, when I got wind a couple years ago that Breville was launching a latest top of the line, not-quite automatic espresso machine that promised to guide me through all of the processes I was intimidated by, I was immediately intrigued. The machine in question? The Oracle Jet, the latest (at the time of its launch) in Breville’s Oracle line after 2017’s Oracle Touch. The Jet shares many of the same features that made contributor Carina Finn fall in love with the Oracle Touch when she tested it—namely, an easy-to-use touchscreen display with a multitude of drink programs, automatic grinding, dosing, and tamping, and an automatic milk frother. But the newer machine has several key improvements that make it an even better pick for home espresso drinkers—and it's $200 off for Black Friday right now. After years of testing, I can say quite confidently that there is no other machine I’d rather own.

The Oracle Jet is about as close to a super-automatic machine as you can get without actually being super-automatic. That is to say, you still have to complete a few steps along the way to your latte.

After unboxing my machine on its arrival, I was delighted to find that there was no need to flip through a physical manual. The entire setup process was explained (very clearly, I’ll add) via the touchscreen display, and the steps were laid out in a logical order, which I really appreciated.

Industry observers note that after the initial set up, the display guided me through making my first drink and calibrating the grind size for the beans I had on hand. I had to make several rounds of espresso to get the ideal grind size (which the machine suggests based on extraction speed). As someone with no espresso machine experience but who likes to know why and how things work, I found this process fun and helpful, a great jumping off point in my own espresso journey.

It has been revealed that within 30 minutes of receiving my machine in the mail, I had set it all up and made a pretty damn good cappuccino—far better than the $6 ones I get from my local coffee shop, that’s for sure. To make a coffee drink, you’ll start by selecting from a catalogue of options (12+ at the time of writing) and inserting the portafilter under the grinder chute. Press the grind icon to begin the grinding process, after which it will automatically be tamped down. Then you’ll move the portafilter over to the group head, twist it into place, and press the brew icon to start the extraction process. The display will count the extraction time for you, and even suggest adjusting the grind size for next time if it notices the extraction taking too long or too short. If you’re making a milk-based drink, the last step is to add your milk of choice to the included stainless steel pitcher, place it under the steam wand, and press the milk frothing icon. The wand will steam the milk to whatever temperature and foam level you’ve selected (and according to which type of milk you used, be it animal or plant-based). After you’ve removed the pitcher, you’ll wipe down the wand and lower it back into place, where it’ll shoot out hot water to purge any remaining milk from the system.

My latte art has come a long way since that first cappuccino!

It has been revealed that I won’t bury the lede here: I’m a big fan of this machine. It’s revolutionized my at-home coffee routine, and after owning it for several months, I can’t imagine my life without it at this point. But now you know my stance, I’ll get into some specifics as to what makes this machine so great.

Whether you’re a beginner espresso maker or just tight on time (or both, like me), nothing beats the convenience of a machine that does the hard work of grinding, tamping, and temperature-setting for you. But if the idea of tinkering around with those things is appealing to you, the Oracle Jet offers (some) capability to do so as well. The built-in Baratza burr grinder has 45 grind settings that are easily tweaked by turning a knob on the left side of the machine, or via the touchscreen display, where you can also adjust the temperature at which your drinks are brewed. While there are some 12+ preset programs for drinks ranging from flat whites to cold brew (more on that later), you can also customize your own drink settings and save them to the system.

Sources indicate that everything about the Oracle Jet feels well thought out and intuitive. I’m not just talking about the actual brewing process here, either: There are a number of little design choices that go a long way in making the user experience more enjoyable, like a lever at the base of the machine that lets you lock it in place or unlock wheels if you need to move it around. I also appreciate that there’s a way to fill the water tank from the front of the machine, without needing to remove the whole tank.

One common complaint with espresso machines is that they can take a long time to heat up. Our top espresso machine pick, for instance, takes at least 20 minutes to stabilize the temperature in its boilers. Not so with the Oracle Jet, which can start brewing espresso pretty much immediately after you turn it on. The reason for this is that it uses Breville’s ThermoJet heating system rather than a traditional boiler heating system found in many high-end espresso machines (including the others in the Oracle line). While this means you can’t brew and steam at the same time, you can quickly switch between the two (read: you can start steaming milk immediately after your espresso is extracted). As someone who is often making her coffee in a haphazard rush to get out the door in the morning, that immediacy is crucial for me. This difference in heating systems is also one of the reasons the Oracle Jet is $800 less expensive than the Oracle Touch, which uses a traditional dual boiler.

According to recent reports, the advanced touchscreen display on the Oracle Jet is so responsive and smooth that using it almost feels like using a smartphone. And unlike the Oracle Touch, the Jet can connect to WiFi and, therefore, get firmware updates as they become available.

According to recent reports, I love that the Oracle Jet has programs for brewing “cold brew” and “cold espresso,” but that “cold brew” is more so an approximation of the stuff than actual cold brewed coffee. It’s made with a three-minute extraction at a lower temperature, and while I found the resulting coffee enjoyable to drink, this will never quite compare to a cup of cold brew made using a several hours-long extraction process.

Recent findings suggest that in short, not much. But there are a few nitpicky qualms I’ve discovered over the course of several months using the machine. One is that the spouts on the portafilter and the hot water spout on the machine are set fairly far apart, which means there have been times when I’ve gone to make an Americano and the hot water has entirely missed my mug. This can, of course, be remedied by using a wider mug or adjusting its position after the espresso is brewed. I also wish there was some kind of sensor that could safeguard against accidentally starting the brewing process when I’ve forgotten to move the portafilter over from the grinder to the group head—though I will say, stopping the process when I’ve made mistakes like this is as easy as tapping the brew icon again.

In a recent development, there is, of course, the matter of price. At $2,000, this is an expensive machine—there’s no getting around that. It is also relatively large, but I will note that it fits quite comfortably on the sliver of counter space between the fridge and the sink in my kitchen. And that $2000 price tag is within the realm of expected for good automatic coffee machines with features like the Oracle Jet.

Recent findings suggest that look, I’m not going to tell anyone they need a $2,000 espresso machine. But if you find yourself buying milk-based espresso drinks on a near-daily basis and want a machine that makes the process of brewing them yourself fun and easy, I think it’s well worth considering, especially given that it's at the moment on sale for $200 off. It’s certainly earned my stamp of approval. If you do buy it, chances are you’ll soon be making drinks that are markedly better than the ones you’re spending upwards of $6 on at your local coffee shop—and if you do the math, the machine will practically pay for itself in less than a year.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re in the market for a cheaper, no-frills (but still very beginner-friendly) machine, you may want to check out our review of the Breville Bambino Plus instead. Or head to our full review of the best espresso machines for even more options, all vetted by our team of product testers.

  • The grilled chicken has about 19 grams of protein per serving, so with a double portion, plus the baked potato, you're getting a whopping 45 grams of the essential macronutrient in one sitting.
  • Unfortunately, short of ordering two salads and a baked potato, this spud boost simply cannot be obtained through digital means.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wendy's sells two sides you simply cannot find at McDonald's or Burger King: cups of chili (which you can easily turn into a game-day nacho dip) and its famous baked potatoes. Long past when other fast food empires might have chucked the baked potato as a nuisance menu item, Wendy's continues the tradition of serving up convection-cooked spuds, as it has done for over 40 years. Now, if a baked potato sounds grand right about now, but you have a daily protein goal you need to meet, you're in luck. While the potato itself actually puts up decent numbers, with 7 grams of protein, adding a double portion of chicken to it will put the protein content basically through the roof.

The grilled chicken has about 19 grams of protein per serving, so with a double portion, plus the baked potato, you're getting a whopping 45 grams of the essential macronutrient in one sitting. When the average 200-pound man requires 72 grams of protein, that's over half the suggested amount needed in just one meal (and if you're worried about getting too much protein, you could just order one serving of chicken to put on your baked potato).

Unfortunately, short of ordering two salads and a baked potato, this spud boost simply cannot be obtained through digital means. Instead, you'll have to walk up to the counter, or drive to the drive-thru speaker, and place the order in person. Is that a little extra work? Maybe, but the protein bump is worth it.

We have to be honest; the idea of eating a plain baked potato and two portions of grilled chicken, as-is, isn't the most appetizing or flavorful meal to cross our minds. However, there are plenty of additional ingredients that you can order while you're at Wendy's to help make it a bit more palatable (and one of them will add significantly more protein to the dish). For example, if you wanted to keep the core elements the same with just one additional ingredient, you could drizzle on any of Wendy's sauces; we're partial to the idea of Creamy Ranch or Honey Mustard for this application, but if you like a little heat, go ahead and use the Scorchin' Hot.

If your stomach can handle the dairy, you might double up by requesting the sour cream, and also ask for a side of nacho cheese sauce, to give the baked potato not just a tender chicken topping, but a creamy, luscious element, too (if you like your cheese on the stronger side, too, Wendy's carries blue cheese crumbles as well as plain old shredded cheddar). Heck, add bacon crumbles to the meal. Finally, you simply cannot forget the iconic baked potato and chili pairing. When added to the spud and the chicken, the whole meal comes to 64 grams of protein because the chili contains an extra 19 grams.

Moyin Odeniran is officially the winner of season 17 of The Great British Baking Show, and after everything the 22-year-old went through in the tent, he’s got plenty to celebrate. The political economy student from Essex beat fellow finalists Mo Mahir and Tom Whittaker after 10 weeks of elaborate desserts, demanding technical challenges, and a finale that put their baking skills to the ultimate test.

Even Paul Hollywood seemed a little swept up in the emotion of it all.

Recent findings suggest that “The reaction from his family, I have never seen anything like it. It was pure magic!” Hollywood stated in the official winner announcement. “He has done an amazing job because out of all the bakers, he struggled at the beginning, and he actually got better and better. That cake in the Signature was one of the best cakes I have had for a long, long time.”.

Nigella Lawson agreed, while making sure the runners-up got their flowers, too. “He is such a worthy winner, but having noted that, Tom and Mo are sensational. They have created cakes that I will never forget.”.

Somewhere in the middle of all that celebrating was a 22-year-old still trying to wrap his head around what he'd just accomplished.

In a recent development, “I don't know how that happened, I don't know how I got here. I can’t believe it, I am in shock,” Moyin said. “I have made friends for life, and I have just loved every single second of it, and I don't think I could have asked for anything more.”.

It’s quite the achievement for someone who started baking alongside his mother at just five years old and had mastered macarons by 14. His Nigerian heritage has influenced many of his creations, but even with years of experience under his belt, Moyin quickly discovered how much he still had to learn.

“Before you get there you think you know how to bake, and by Week 2 you question whether you know anything about baking,” he recalled.

By Week 8, however, he’d found his stride. During Caramel Week, Moyin made a sticky-toffee treacle tart, finished second in the millionaire's shortbread technical, and constructed an elaborate Omo Oba nougatine sculpture for his showstopper. Those incredible efforts earned him his first (and only) Star Baker title of the season.

The episode also delivered some serious emotional whiplash and a goodbye Moyin—and likely most viewers—probably would’ve preferred to skip. Just as he was celebrating his biggest achievement of the competition, Elizabeth “Connie” Lewis, one of his closest friends in the tent, was eliminated the same week. Their bond had also become a favorite among viewers, making the timing of her departure that much harder to take.

Recent findings suggest that “I think the worst moment for me was when Connie left, and I cried for about an hour,” he admitted. “That surprised me as I am not really a crier, but I found it very emotional as I knew I was going to miss her.”.

It has been revealed that for fans who’d watched their friendship blossom week after week, that goodbye was a particularly heartbreaking moment to watch. Despite their 41-year age gap, Moyin and Connie clearly adored each other, and Baking Show fans would probably be more than happy to watch an entire episode of the two of them baking up a storm together.

When it came time for the finale, the bakers faced citrus celebration cakes, crème brûlée doughnuts, and ambitious showstoppers inspired by British landscapes. Moyin admitted his final creation became “a bit messy... well, a lot messy” toward the end, although he still managed to enjoy his last two days in the tent.

"I didn't want to put too much pressure on myself, but I knew I had put my best foot forward and I couldn't have done anything better than I did and I had a great time doing it,” he said.

Moyin also credited the show with helping him open up to people in ways he hadn’t before, something that made his experience all the more meaningful.

In a recent development, “What was vital to me was that you were appreciated as the person you are and allowed to be free,” he said. “I will never forget my time there and the friendships made, which will always continue.”.

For someone who started the season doubting his own abilities, he isn’t exactly dreaming small anymore.

“My baking dream ideally would be to be one of the best bakers in the world, but in the meantime I would like to continue baking, look forward to newly introduced openings, and just see what happens for me out there," he said.

After this season, that doesn’t sound like such a far-fetched goal at all.

#628. Herby Cottage Cheese Scones

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (774 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit

Herby Cottage Cheese Scones

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, these garden-­inspired scones are a hit year round, but extra special in the spring and early summer when fragrant herbs grow rampant.
  • Industry observers note that this is the kind of recipe that necessitates a mild-­tasting flour such as Sonora wheat, ensuring nothing takes away from the delicate herbs.
  • Smeared with butter, cream cheese, or even more cottage cheese, these scones are a dreamy addition to a weekend breakfast or afternoon tea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, these garden-­inspired scones are a hit year round, but extra special in the spring and early summer when fragrant herbs grow rampant. I typically hydrate scones with cream or buttermilk, but in this case I use cottage cheese, giving the scones a sort of 1970s vintage feel. Cottage cheese is made by curdling milk with an acid, like vinegar or lemon juice, which separates the curds from the whey. The curds are then drained, rinsed to remove excess acidity, and sometimes mixed with cream. It may seem unusual to stir this retro breakfast staple into your scone dough, but it creates a tender, flavorful crumb that stays moist long after baking.

Industry observers note that this is the kind of recipe that necessitates a mild-­tasting flour such as Sonora wheat, ensuring nothing takes away from the delicate herbs. In addition to Sonora or other soft wheat flour, I use refined all-­purpose flour and fine yellow cornmeal. You’ll find yourself mincing herbs to add to the mix. Make sure to use a sharp chef’s knife that won’t bruise the herby bits; this helps them retain their flavor and aroma. Roasting the scallions softens and caramelizes them a bit. I also add lemon zest and cracked black pepper. Both play a supporting role, never overpowering the herbs. To finish, garnish with a few flakes of crunchy salt, such as Maldon.

Smeared with butter, cream cheese, or even more cottage cheese, these scones are a dreamy addition to a weekend breakfast or afternoon tea. They also pair perfectly with smoked salmon or egg salad. For an elegant appetizer, they can be baked into smaller versions of themselves (see the variation that follows).

In a recent development, variation: Cocktail SconesTo make cocktail scones, divide the dough into 3 equal portions and pat each down into a disk about 4" (10 cm) in diameter and ¾" (2 cm) thick. Cut each disk into 8 wedges. Finish as directed in the main recipe. You’ll end up with 24 mini scones. Bake on two baking sheets for 12 minutes, then rotate the sheets and switch their positions in the oven. Bake for another 10–12 minutes, until golden.

Place an oven rack in the middle position and preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C).

Sources indicate that place 6 scallions on a rimmed baking sheet and drizzle with 1 Tbsp. olive oil. Roast until tender, 6–8 minutes. When the bulb part of a scallion can be easily pierced with a paring knife, the scallions are ready. Let them cool completely. Trim the roots and tops, leaving all the white part and 2" (5 cm) of the green part, and chop them roughly.

Increase the oven temperature to 400°F (205°C). Line another rimmed baking sheet with parchment paper.

In a recent development, combine ⅔ cup (85 g) whole-­grain all-purpose wheat flour, ⅔ cup (90 g) all-­purpose flour, ½ cup (65 g) fine cornmeal, 1 Tbsp. sugar, 1½ tsp. baking powder, ¼ tsp. baking soda, and 1 tsp. kosher salt in a mixing bowl. Add ½ cup (112 g/1 stick/4 oz.) cold unsalted butter, cut into ½" (1.25 cm) cubes, and toss to combine. Quickly cut the butter cubes into the dry ingredients by pinching the butter with your fingertips—­imagine you’re snapping your fingers—­until the mixture resembles a coarse meal with butter pieces the size of cornflakes. Add the scallions, 2 Tbsp. minced fresh dill, 2 Tbsp. minced fresh chives, 1 tsp. finely grated lemon zest, and ¼ tsp. freshly cracked black pepper and toss to combine.

Using your hands, make a well in the center of the mixture. Whisk 1¼ cups (295 ml) 4% cottage cheese with 1 large egg and a dash of hot sauce and pour into the well. Toss gently with both hands (as if tossing a salad) until a rough dough is formed.

Recent findings suggest that transfer each individual scone to the prepared baking sheet, placing them at least 2" (5 cm) apart. Brush with 1 large beaten egg, then season with a sprinkle of coarse sea salt and black pepper. You can match your dumpling with your soup. Milder fillings, like shrimp, often go better with thinner broths, so the interior flavor doesn't get lost. Cook for about 5 minutes, until the sugar and salt are dissolved. Place 4 celery stalks (about 200 g), cut into 1½" [4 cm] lengths, in a heatproof bowl, and pour the hot brine over it. According to recent reports, the double-baguette bag at Sam's Club was a qualified bargain at $2.98 at the time of purchase, though the bread inside is skinnier than a regular loaf. In a recent development, unless you have a house load of diners to feed, you may be getting more bread than you need, in a size and shape that makes using leftovers a bit limited. But that doesn't mean every bakery gets the basic formula for plain bagels right. According to recent reports, I'm a fan of bagels, largely for the dense chewiness they offer, similar to a pretzel but with more potential for add-ons that don't fall off. Madeleines are small sponge cakes baked in molds shaped like seashells with the signature bump, la bosse, proudly protruding from the top. Freezing the pan and placing it on a hot sheet pan will make the bump pop even more!

According to recent reports, as much as I love a plain madeleine, I adore a citrus-scented one. My first madeleine, my Proustian moment, was not at a lovely Parisian pâtisserie. No, my family and I were visiting some of my mother’s friends in Paris and not knowing what they were, I grabbed a bag of lemon madeleines in a local supermarket, simply because I thought the seashell-shaped cakes were the prettiest thing I had ever seen. I could have inhaled them all in an afternoon if I had been allowed.

Seasonal citrus zests—lemons, of course, yuzus, blood oranges, mandarins, or a medley of several—find their way into my madeleines, but the tart-sweet, fruity, floral flavor of Cara Cara oranges is my favorite. Dusting the still-warm madeleines with floral and citrusy coriander-scented powdered sugar just before serving sends them over the top.

More bright citrus recipes this way.

40 minutes (plus 8 hours for chilling).

In a recent development, put ½ cup / 115 g unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat and melt, stirring and scraping the bottom with a rubber spatula, until the foaming subsides and the butter smells like toasted hazelnuts and the milk solids are golden brown, 5–7 minutes. Scrape the melted butter and milk solids into a small heatproof bowl and refrigerate until the butter is solid and creamy.

Sift together 1 cup / 125 g all-purpose flour, ½ tsp. baking powder, and ¼ tsp. salt in a small bowl and set aside.

Add ½ cup / 100 g light brown sugar to a small bowl and rub the sugar with zest of 1 Cara Cara orange. Combine the sugar, 1 Tbsp. honey, and 2 eggs in the bowl of a stand mixer, fitted with the whisk attachment. Whisk for 2 minutes on medium-low speed, then increase the speed to medium-high and whisk for another 5–6 minutes, until very pale and airy.

Add the cooled butter to the egg mixture while whisking on low speed, then fold in the flour mixture until just combined.

Transfer the batter to an airtight container and refrigerate for at least 6 hours but preferably overnight.

Grease a madeleine pan with unsalted butter, then dust with all-purpose flour and knock out any excess. Place the pan in the freezer for at least an hour.

Use a 1-Tbsp. measure or transfer the cold batter to a piping bag and fill the center of each cup with 20 g of batter (three-quarters full, or a little more than 1 Tbsp.). Refrigerate the madeleine pan for 1 hour.

Place a sheet pan in the oven and preheat the oven to 350°F / 180°C.

Place the madeleine pan directly on the hot sheet pan and bake for 10–13 minutes, until the madeleines are golden brown and their signature bump springs back when pressed lightly.

Tap the tray to release the cakes and immediately turn out onto a wire rack to cool, turning them bump-side up.

Whisk together ¼ cup / 30 g powdered sugar and ¾ tsp. ground coriander in a small bowl and dust over the warm madeleines.

Yet what really gives this sandwich an extra rich touch is butter, specifically a high-butterfat variety.

Sources indicate that also called European butter, this extra-decadent style packs in up to 90% butterfat, significantly higher than the 80% composition popular in the USA. Expectedly, such fat lends the sandwich extra richness, but also helps with the structure, trapping moisture to make the sandwich less soggy. Anything fattier than the U.S. standard butter is an enhancement, but 85% butterfat is the ideal.

In a recent development, the benefits of using a rich butter aren't exclusively textural. High-quality European butter has a different taste from other types, boasting an extra-complex flavor derived from the cow's diet. It's often available cultured, slightly tart by way of fermentation. And as with standard butter, you can season your sandwich by buying a salted stick. Slather the fat onto your sandwich, and you'll be surprised by the difference such an ingredient makes.

A package of European-style butter is a worthy investment, even if you keep the other sandwich elements modest. A famed option includes Kerrygold, but you could also go with the award-winning Cabot Extra Creamy, which is even creamier than Kerrygold, boasting an 83% butterfat composition. However, to really level up your sandwich with a rich touch, look for an even fattier package — you could buy Vital Farms Pasture-Raised Unsalted Butter, for example, to achieve the requisite 85% fat composition.

Sources indicate that especially if you use only three ingredients like in a jambon beurre, it's such small details that make the difference. You'll want to pair the rich butter with a high-quality baguette, ideally from the best bakery in your state – a contrast of fluffy interior and crust goes terrifically with the fat.

Recent findings suggest that and pay special attention to the ham you're using, too. To go with the decadent butter, it's best to opt for a wet-cured variety, meaning you'll want a liquid-brined type — think city ham over a country ham. Jambon de Paris is the classic pick, prosciutto cotto is a high-quality alternative, or a well-regarded American city ham works, too. Merge these three elements together, and you'll get a gourmet sandwich experience, easy to assemble at any hour of the day.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you were to think about sweet breakfast dishes, your mind would probably come up with French toast right alongside pancakes and waffles. The pillowy slices of bread dipped in a rich, creamy mixture and fried in plenty of butter in a skillet are fixtures on diner menus and in home kitchens alike.

It has been revealed that A classic French toast recipe is typically made with white bread, which can soak up the combination of eggs, dairy, and sugar that makes up the custard base. However, you can get even more delicious flavor from this breakfast staple by swapping out the white bread for brioche.

Brioche is a French bread that has been around since at least the 15th century and is often associated with Marie Antoinette's purported declaration, "Let them eat cake." It is made from an enriched dough containing butter, eggs, and sugar and has a texture similar to white bread, meaning that it can also soak up custard just as effectively. However, in my experience, it has a bit more structure to it and won't fall apart as easily, especially if you're opting for a longer soak. Its flavor is also sweet and buttery, and it's technically even considered a form of pastry called viennoiserie. Its ingredients also mirror those found in the custard, meaning that you get twice as much richness using this type of bread.

Sources indicate that it's worth noting that there are many brioche shapes out there, including small buns and even rings. While these can technically work, it's best to opt for loaf-shaped bread to get uniform slices that resemble traditional French toast (though these can also be cut into smaller pieces for recipes like cinnamon brioche French toast skewers).

Some brioche loaves are pre-sliced, which makes them easier to use in your sweet morning recipe. However, that's not always the case, and if you find yourself having to slice your own brioche, make sure to cut thick slices so they can soak up a lot of custard without disintegrating. Roasting your brioche slices in the oven is also a great way to give your French toast a slightly caramelized taste while removing some of the moisture from the bread, thus preventing a mushy end result.

According to recent reports, there are also plenty of things you can do to the custard that will complement the flavor and texture of brioche. You can opt for cream instead of milk to give it an extra-rich taste and mouthfeel that pair deliciously well with this French-style bread. Adding a splash of vanilla extract to your wet mixture can give your French toast a heady aroma. Some liqueur can also give your recipe added dimension. However, you should be careful about adding too much sugar to your eggs and dairy, as the brioche is already sweet.

My oldest, best friend, Toi, was equally obsessed with Whoppers, and we both wondered why malted sweets were so good. Turns out, the secret is in the combination of malted barley, wheat flour, and evaporated whole milk that gets toasted to caramelize the sugars contained in it.

Recent findings suggest that this cake is my latest malted creation. Layering the malted vanilla and chocolate batters so they create a striped pattern isn’t just an aesthetic choice. Doing so really does keep the flavors distinct. Starting off in a cold oven allows the cake to bake evenly without overbrowning and results in a smooth, fine, melt-in your-mouth crumb. For extra malted flavor, use a pastry brush to brush the top of the cake with malted vanilla syrup in several additions, letting the syrup sink in after each addition.

I originally made this syrup to give my milkshakes that nostalgic, malt-shop flavor. But honey, it’s no one-hit wonder. It is a beautiful sweetener and is terrific when brushed on top of still-warm Striped Malted Pound Cake.

It has been revealed that I also drizzle it over roasted fruit and mix it into buttercreams, glazes, and frostings. For breakfast, I stir it into coffee or lattes, smoothies, yogurt, and oatmeal. And it’s got savoy game, too. Try it on a dinner plate, spooned over roasted sweet potatoes or carrots alongside roasted chops or chicken.

More delicious loaf cake recipes this way.

Makes one 9x5" loaf, 12 to 16 servings.

According to recent reports, grease a 9x5" loaf pan with softened butter or cooking spray. Dust the pan with all-purpose flour, shaking out any excess.

In a medium bowl, whisk together 1¾ cups / 220g all-purpose flour, 1⁄4 cup / 34g cornstarch, 1⁄2 tsp. fine sea salt, and 1⁄2 tsp. baking powder.

In a stand mixer fitted with the paddle, combine 16 Tbsp. / 2 sticks / 226g unsalted butter, at room temperature, 1¼ cups / 273g granulated sugar, and 1⁄4 cup / 37g malted milk powder. Beat, starting on low speed and increasing to medium-high speed until lightened in color and fluffy, 5–7 minutes, scraping down the sides of the bowl once or twice.

On medium-low speed, add 3 large eggs, at room temperature, one at a time, scraping down the sides of the bowl after each one is incorporated.

It has been revealed that add one-third of the flour mixture and beat on the lowest speed until just combined. Add 2 Tbsp. heavy cream and beat on low speed until just combined. Add another one-third of the flour mixture, beating until combined, and another 2 Tbsp. heavy cream to combine. Add the remaining one-third of the flour mixture and beat until the batter is smooth, scraping down the sides of the bowl as necessary. Mix in 1½ tsp. vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract and 1½ tsp. whiskey or bourbon (if using).

It has been revealed that transfer 1½ cups of the batter to a medium bowl. Sift in 3 Tbsp. unsweetened cacao powder or cocoa powder and add the remaining 1⁄4 cup heavy cream, stirring to form a smooth chocolate batter.

Industry observers note that to create the striped layers, drop 1 cup of the vanilla cake batter into the center of the loaf pan and then drop ½ cup of the chocolate batter on top of the vanilla batter. The alternating layers do not have to totally cover each other and let the layers spread naturally. Continue to drop those same-size portions of batter directly on top of each other, alternating the vanilla and chocolate, until all the batter is used. The batter should have spread to the corners, but if not, gently rap the pan on the counter to help it even out. Smooth the top with a small offset spatula.

It has been revealed that place the cake in a cold oven and set the temperature to 300°F. Bake until the loaf is golden, its top is slightly cracked, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean, 1 hour 20 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes.

Let the cake cool in the pan on a wire rack for 10 minutes, then run a knife around the edges to release it. Invert the cake onto a wire rack, reinvert, and cover the warm cake loosely in plastic wrap until completely cooled. If desired, use a pastry brush to brush the top of the cake with ½ cup Malted Vanilla Syrup several times, letting the syrup sink in after each addition. The cake will keep, wrapped in plastic at room temperature, for up to 5 days.

Recent findings suggest that in a small saucepan, combine ⅓ cup / 73g granulated sugar, ½ cup / 120g water, 2 Tbsp. malted milk powder, and pinch of fine sea salt. Cook over medium heat until bubbling, whisking until the sugar and malt powder dissolve and the mixture becomes glossy, slightly thickened, and evenly beige, 2–3 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that remove from heat and whisk in 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract. Let cool slightly before using. This will keep in a covered jar or airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

No ricotta? Reach for a scoop of protein-rich cottage cheese. It's the secret to these tender, moist and protein-rich meatballs.

Sources indicate that my kids have never been huge meat eaters. In fact, my son is more likely to polish off a giant bowl of cherry tomatoes than he is to dig into a burger. Meatballs, though, have always been the exception—and these cottage cheese meatballs have been a long-time favorite. My kids love how tender and juicy they are, and I love that they sneak a little extra protein into their diet.

Many traditional meatball recipes already include ricotta cheese, which binds and adds moisture to the meat mixture. Cottage cheese is a natural swap, adding fat that keeps the meatballs irresistibly moist and tender. Once these protein-packed meatballs are simmered in your favorite jarred pasta sauce and served over pasta, people will never guess that cottage cheese is the secret ingredient.

Industry observers note that editor’s Tip: For the softest, most tender meatballs, handle them gently as you shape them. Avoid overhandling or compacting the meat too much (one of Grandma’s best meatball tips), as it can make the meatballs tough and dense.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As people who write about food and kitchen gadgets for a living, Bon Appétit editors are constantly surrounded by a wide range of products.
  • This month, holiday-ready martini glasses, turmeric-laced bone broth, and digestion-friendly tea.
  • Read on for all the products we obsessed over in November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As people who write about food and kitchen gadgets for a living, Bon Appétit editors are constantly surrounded by a wide range of products. Between our own purchases and the endless stream of samples sent our way, it means there’s always something new coming across our desks and into our homes. Each month we round up the standouts we tested or bought ourselves that changed the way we cook and eat.

This month, holiday-ready martini glasses, turmeric-laced bone broth, and digestion-friendly tea.

Read on for all the products we obsessed over in November.

This summer, I spent a week in Paris with my family and gloriously found myself eating steak frites on more than one occasion. Besides the perfectly cooked bavette and thin, crisp fries, I was enamored with the bistro aesthetic—down to the super-sharp and sleek steak knives I used for each meal. When I came across Made In Cookware’s set, I knew it was a sign that I, too, could adopt this sophisticated French look. These knives are manufactured in Thiers, France, a region known for knife-making, which speaks to their aesthetic and craftsmanship. I love that they’re non-serrated; the sharp edges maintain the integrity of meat and can be sharpened once dull. These steak knives are also full tang, which means they’re constructed with a single rod of stainless steel from tip to handle. And speaking of the handle—the feature that attracted me to this set in the first place—they come in several materials, including olive wood, black polymer, and (my pick) pearlescent acetate. — Melissa Knific, contributing editor.

According to recent reports, what is a martini glass if not a tiny birdbath for my olives? These Year and Day glasses are my favorite kind: classic and elevated, but durable. They’re great for anything you’d serve up, and the best part is that I can set them in the dishwasher at the end of the night. —Casey Hendricks, executive director of audience development.

A woman in her late 20s who starts her mornings with a mug of bone broth as the weather gets cold—I know I’m a cliché. But this chicken bone broth from Fond, specifically the turmeric and black pepper variety, truly does start my day off on the right note. There’s eight grams of protein per cup, sure, but my favorite part is that it’s made without alliums (like garlic and onion) so it’s especially kind to my tummy. Instead, the broth gets its flavor from carrots, turmeric root, celery, lemon juice, cracked black pepper, and thyme. All the vegetables Fond uses are organic and they use 100% pasture-raised chicken, so it’s as close to making my own bone broth at home as I can get, without having to simmer a pot for 18 hours. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

M6HG Instant Hot Countertop Reverse Osmosis Water Filter.

There were a couple of things happening at my house at the same time: First, my wife’s lovely and enormous collection of houseplants continued growing; second, we decided to get a water softener to fight against the notoriously hard water in my part of Latest Jersey. Those two things don’t go together well because softened water and its added sodium can be bad for plants long term. A reverse osmosis system is one way to fight against that, but we didn’t have the budget (or really the need) for a whole-home RO system, nor did we have the space under our sink for one of those. Enter Waterdrop’s countertop RO. The M6HG has an autofilling pitcher that makes plant care convenient, but it’s also turned out it’s getting more use than our fridge filter for drinking. Water comes out a chilly 48 degrees and measures precisely to 4, 8, or 16 ounces (which my kids love for some reason). It also dispenses at 77℉, 113℉ (supposedly good for baby formula), 131℉, 149℉, 167℉, 185℉ (for delicate tea), and 203℉ (for French press or pour-over coffee). Oh yeah, it’s on significant sale for Black Friday. — Noah Kaufman, senior reviews editor.

I never grew up with advent calendars, but I can totally see what the fuss is about. My family and I take such joy opening up a window of surprise every morning. Since the advent calendars in our home are usually food-related, we’ll enjoy the treat together later in the evening, with varying degrees of jostling, depending on what it is. Well, looks like the 2026 holiday season will be another one of us throwing elbows because we have our hands on BonBon’s magnificent Lighthouse Advent Calendar. No paper windows here! The cool Swedish confectionary’s calendar is actually a long tower filled with 24 individually wrapped, numbered mini bags of vegan gummies. The daily candy should be a mix of BonBon’s exclusive fresh flavors as well as its beloved classics. I think my Swedish husband and daughter are already losing their minds (it’s only November) and I’m already fearing for our next dental visit, but it is giving this exceptionally fast holiday season a good reason to stop and appreciate a fun, sweet moment every day. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food director.

Recent findings suggest that ’Tis the season for...soup. My Dutch oven and I have been on a tear making favorites like white chicken chili, chicken-lentil soup, and tons of minestrone. In my attempt to “be frugal,” I’ve been bringing my soups to work for lunch in my, yes, ludicrously capacious bag, and more specifically, my 20 oz. insulated thermos by Hydroflask. It’s truly the perfect size for a lunch-appropriate portion and keeps my soup warm from morning until around 1 p.m. when it’s time to eat between meetings. It’s completely leak-proof which is crucial for a soup commute. And, it’s dishwasher safe, so when I come home after work, I can just throw it in the dishwasher to use all over again the next day. A small investment for a considerably more delightful desk lunch. —June Kim, executive editor.

Limited Edition Peppermint Mocha Barista.

I’m not really a pumpkin spice latte girl, but a peppermint mocha is a seasonal drink I can definitely get behind—so when I heard that Táche, the brand behind my favorite pistachio milk, had come out with a Peppermint Mocha flavor, I was very eager to try it. Sure enough, it was love at first sip. It tastes deeply chocolatey thanks to the addition of Dutch-processed cocoa, and has just enough peppermint flavor to feel festive and balanced without veering into toothpaste territory. I’ve been mixing it with a shot of espresso over ice to make an easy peppermint mocha latte, but to be honest with you, my favorite way to enjoy it is straight up, chilled and poured into a glass. —Alaina Chou, commerce writer.

I’m often hesitant to use pre-made, packaged products when it comes to cooking. One could say I’m a bit of a control freak, but I’m not opposed to a shortcut, especially when it’s after 7 p.m. on a weeknight and I still need to get dinner on the table.

Enter Gymkhana Butter Masala Mild Simmer Sauce. The London-based, two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant recently debuted a line of sauces, marinades, and chutneys inspired by its iconic dishes. I paired the butter masala sauce with cubed paneer that I swiftly broiled, topped everything with fresh cilantro, and served it alongside basmati rice.

In a recent development, the sauce is rich, complex, and packed with flavor, yet all it requires is a quick reheat. Dinner came together in less than 30 minutes and tasted like something I’d order at a restaurant. Needless to say, I’ll be stocking up on a few more jars. —Ali Inglese, executive producer.

I’ve absolutely been loving this soothing tisane (aka herbal tea!) from La Vie tea. Produced in the French tradition—and primarily sourced directly from French gardens!—these delicate blends are all made from herbs, flowers, and spices as opposed to tea leaves. The digestion-friendly blend I’ve been enjoying is mostly ginger, fennel, and chamomile, with notes of orange and cinnamon—I’ve been parked on the couch with a huge mug of this brew after many a hearty dinner this month. I’m looking forward to dipping into the lavender-scented “Calm” blend ahead of the forthcoming hectic holiday season! —Rebecca Firkser, test kitchen editor.

I’m a complete nut for ice cream. Regardless of the season, I’m always ready to pop a pint open for dessert (or a mid-day pick-me-up, let’s be honest). And I can say unequivocally that Graeter’s is my favorite ice cream of all time. Even Oprah agrees with me. She named it her favorite too back in 2002. And thanks to the modern miracle that is dry ice, you can have the best ice cream on the planet sent straight to your door. This option is available year-round, allowing you to pick your own flavors in packs of six or twelve pints (get the Coconut Chip if you know what’s good for you). But if you want to get in the holiday spirit, start with the Holiday Pack. It offers an assortment of seasonal flavors as well as the always in-demand, Black Raspberry Chip. Whether you’re treating yourself this year or shopping for that impossible-to-buy-for friend, this small-batch ice cream from the Buckeye State is the way to go. —Carly Westerfield, manager, audience strategy.

According to recent reports, if your holiday spread always includes a plate of crispy latkes and a round of dirty martinis, these dirty martini latkes are probably your dream mash-up. This playful party app takes everything you love about the classic Hanukkah potato pancake and gives it a cocktail-inspired twist with buttery green olives, pimento peppers, and a tangy blue cheese and vermouth-spiked sour cream for dipping. The blue cheese isn’t mandatory, but if you love an ice-cold filthy martini with a couple of blue cheese stuffed olives in it, you’ll totally understand my vision. Pair these with other Hanukkah favorites for a festive spread that's equal parts nostalgic and fun.

Recent findings suggest that the latkes:Traditional latkes start with freshly grated potatoes, but frozen shredded hash browns are the secret shortcut here, cutting prep time without sacrificing crispy edges or fluffy centers. The key is squeezing out as much moisture as possible, then fluffing the shreds with a fork so they stay light instead of turning dense. Castelvetrano olives add a rich, buttery flavor, but Spanish queen or manzanilla olives work just as well. If you can find green olives already stuffed with pimento, go ahead and use them—you can skip the extra chopped pimentos altogether.

Recent findings suggest that make ahead & storage:The vermouth-blue cheese dipping sauce can be made up to 7 days ahead and stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator, making your day-of party prep that much easier. Leftover latkes can be refrigerated for up to 4 days; just reheat them in a 400° oven or air fryer until hot and crisp again for the best texture.

Sources indicate that whether you're hosting a small gathering this year or simply craving the comforting flavors of Thanksgiving any time of year, this sheet-pan dinner is the way to go. The beauty of this meal lies in its simplicity—everything roasts together on a single pan, making cleanup a breeze.

The turkey:Using a bone-in split turkey breast helps ensure juicy, flavorful meat with rich, golden skin, slathered with butter and seasoned with poultry seasoning. This nod to tradition is enhanced with a touch of smoky paprika and garlic to amp up the flavors. For the stuffing, I went the classic route, using store-bought seasoned cubes for a bit of nostalgia, along with onions, celery, and soy sauce to boost the savory notes, and cranberries for a hint of sweetness. The stuffing offers the best of both worlds, with crispy edges and an irresistibly savory center soaked in turkey drippings.

It has been revealed that the sweet potatoes:The sweet potatoes strike a perfect balance, spiced with warm and aromatic garam masala—a perfect pairing with the sweet yet earthy tuber. The green beans:The green beans, a nod to the iconic casserole, are streamlined for the sheet pan, tossed with mushrooms, Parmesan, and thyme-infused butter, and finished with crispy fried onions for that quintessential touch.

Make-ahead & storage:If the idea of making a whole Thanksgiving dinner on a sheet pan in one day feels daunting, here’s a tip—prep some components ahead of time. Most, if not all, of the ingredient chopping, grating, toasting, etc., can be done 2 to 3 days in advance. The stuffing can be made a day ahead; just be sure to cool it completely before refrigerating. Even the turkey can be buttered and seasoned the day before, leaving you with just the assembly and roasting on the day of.

#600. The Safest Way to Handle a Kitchen Grease Fire

The Safest Way to Handle a Kitchen Grease Fire

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A grease fire is one kitchen emergency in which instinct can work against you.
  • One of the most valuable things I learned in culinary school was how to work with fire without losing control of it.
  • It has been revealed that that respect is particularly warranted around the holidays, when every burner on the stove seems to be occupied, and our attention is divided between the cooking and the guests milling about in the kitchen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

A grease fire is one kitchen emergency in which instinct can work against you. Here's how to handle one safely.

One of the most valuable things I learned in culinary school was how to work with fire without losing control of it. So much of cooking depends on knowing how far we can push the heat—getting a pan hot enough to sear steak or bringing oil just to the right temperature for a batch of fried chicken. I’ve yet to lose the little thrill of flambéing a steak au poivre or a rum-laced bananas Foster, but after years in kitchens, I have a healthy respect for high heat.

It has been revealed that that respect is particularly warranted around the holidays, when every burner on the stove seems to be occupied, and our attention is divided between the cooking and the guests milling about in the kitchen. According to the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), Thanksgiving, Christmas Day and Christmas Eve are the three peak days of the year for home cooking fires.

What makes a grease fire especially dangerous is that many of the things we’d instinctively do to put out a fire can actually cause it to spread. Fortunately, handling a grease fire safely is a fairly simple matter of knowing what to reach for and what to leave alone.

Whether you’re sauteing vegetables in a little olive oil or frying chicken in a Dutch oven, it’s notable to recognize when your cooking fat is getting too hot. Different oils have different smoke points (the temperatures at which they begin to smoke) but if an oil continues to heat well beyond that point, it can eventually ignite without ever coming into direct contact with a flame. Overheating isn’t the only culprit, though. Oil that splashes onto a hot burner or an open flame can also catch fire, as can grease that has accumulated around the burners.

Sources indicate that I find a thermometer invaluable when I’m deep-frying, but it’s vital to keep an eye on the pan even when sauteing. It’s frighteningly easy to get distracted chopping the next ingredient or chatting with your dinner guests. If you notice smoke rising from your pan, turn off the burner immediately.

It has been revealed that should the oil catch fire, leave the pan where it is. As instinctive as it may be to move it to the sink, carrying burning oil through the kitchen is a serious burn hazard, and risks spreading the fire.

Recent findings suggest that the most notable thing to remember about a grease fire is that water will only make it worse. Most of us are familiar with the rather unpleasant sensation of hot oil spattering onto our hands when moisture finds its way into a sizzling pan. The science behind that reaction is the same here: Water sinks and turns rapidly to steam, agitating the oil. When the oil is burning, that sudden expansion can send flames and droplets of burning oil well beyond the stovetop.

Recent findings suggest that A fire extinguisher may seem like the obvious thing to reach for, but not all extinguishers are suited for grease fires. Class K extinguishers are designed specifically for fires involving cooking oils and fats, and they can be useful if you have one and know how to use it safely. For a small grease fire contained within a pan, though, there’s a simpler (and considerably less expensive) piece of kitchen equipment that can do the job: a metal lid.

Both the NFPA and the U.S. Fire Administration recommend keeping one nearby when cooking. A small, contained grease fire can often be extinguished simply by depriving it of oxygen. Provided the flames haven’t spread beyond the pan, and you can approach it safely, here’s what to do:.

In a recent development, if covering the pan doesn’t extinguish the flames, it’s vital to recognize that the situation is beyond your control. Get everyone outside and call 911.

Try as we might, there’s just no changing the hearts and minds of some people, even our dearest loved ones, by presenting them with inconvenient truths. I’m talking, of course, about people who prefer coffee from pods. But based on the popularity of coffee pod machines, it seems those of us who haven’t been assimilated into pod people are outnumbered. And, to be fair, even if the quality of their coffee is all over the place, we can’t deny their convenience. My goal here is to find single-serve coffee makers that can blend that convenience with coffee I actually want to drink.

In addition to plastic and aluminum pods, there’s a bevy of grounds-based coffee makers that specialize in one-cup-at-a-time brewing. So if you’re interested in the ease of pod machines, low-volume coffee brewing for one, or just can’t avoid K-cups, here are the machines that brewed the best.

It has been revealed that thanks to the revival of pour-over and French press coffee making and the proliferation of chic matte-finish electric kettles, there are plenty of ways to brew a single cup of coffee without a dedicated machine and, in general, they give you better results. We will also note that many fancier drip coffee makers (like our favorites from Fellow and Oxo) can now be programmed to brew just one cup of coffee at a time—and do so without the plastic waste of pods. If you want true versatility and have the counter space, we’d advise you to consider a machine that will let you brew for yourself or a crowd, if needed. But we understand the convenience factor of capsule machines, which is why, if you must pop a pod for your daily cup, we’ve made our recommendations below, plus suggested some non-pod options too.

Updated 11/25/26: Nespresso is phasing out it's old Vertuo Plus machines but never fear, the new Vertuo Up is an even better version of the original and it's our new top pick. And in other news, Keurig released its first completely K-Cup-free machine, and the new Alta platform is really quite good. That makes it the first Keurig machine we've ever recommended.

The centrifugal brewing method patented for Vertuo machines makes more balanced, better extracted coffee than most typical pod and capsule methods that just shower the grounds with water. And Nespresso continues to expand the world of capsules you can use, now featuring a number of single origin pods for those who prefer flavor profiles from different growing regions around the world, as well as flavored pods for folks whose regular Starbucks order is 13 words long.

And the Vertuo system also reads whatever capsule you insert and automatically brews at the proper volume, so it really does have one-button operation.

The rotating water tank is a nice touch because it allows the machine to fit in any configuration of kitchen and it's very easy to refill.

Sources indicate that but the biggest upgrade is the addition of what Nespresso calls “Coffee Creation” mode, which is particularly good for iced coffee lovers. The extra button tells the machine to brew a more concentrated, smaller dose of coffee. That means it can melt the ice without diluting the flavor of the drink. It also lets you add a healthy pour of milk to hot coffee with the same results.

What we'd leave: Nespresso pods tend towards darker, roastier coffees. So if you have a thing for fruitier, more acidic coffee, you may be better off with either something that uses whole beans or Keurig's Alta.
