📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that thanksgiving is known for plenty of traditions, from arguing over who makes the best mac and cheese to fighting for the last slice of pie. But there’s another tradition that's becoming increasingly popular.

Industry observers note that if you've ever been at Thanksgiving dinner when a group of cousins suddenly reveals they're going for a walk, you probably know what's happening. The so-called “cousin walk,” when relatives sneak away to smoke weed, has become such a recognizable holiday ritual that it's now inspiring TikTok videos, memes, and an entire shopping event.

Enter Green Wednesday, the cannabis industry’s answer to Black Friday.

Sources indicate that green Wednesday is the day before Thanksgiving, and it has become one of the year’s biggest shopping days for cannabis retailers. This year, it falls on November 25.

The term has been around since at least 2016, when cannabis delivery manufacturer Eaze began using it after noticing a surge in purchases ahead of Thanksgiving.

According to MJBizDaily, cannabis retailers recorded approximately $138.5 million in sales on Green Wednesday in 2025, up from $132.4 million the previous year, based on data from cannabis market intelligence tech giant BDSA.

While Green Wednesday is often described as the industry’s second-biggest shopping day behind 4/20, some retailers are seeing even stronger results.

According to data RISE Dispensaries shared with Delish, Green Wednesday was its biggest sales day of 2025 and outperformed the notorious cannabis holiday 4/20. The company’s sales were roughly double an average Wednesday, while pre-rolls saw their strongest sales day of the year.

A major part of Green Wednesday’s cultural appeal comes from the infamous cousin walk—the tradition has become a recurring joke across social media, with TikTok users sharing videos about coordinating their annual walkabout. And, of course, brands are getting involved, too.

Industry observers note that as Morning Brew reported, Jif referenced cousin walks in an Instagram promotion last year, while a Taco Bell and Hidden Valley collaboration played on a similar holiday joke. Cannabis brand Dogwalkers is also leaning into the tradition with a Cousin Walk Kit tied to Thanksgiving.

And while Green Wednesday and the cousin walk go hand in hand, cannabis use isn't limited to just the cousins.

Industry observers note that A 2026 study from UC San Diego found that approximately 8.9% of Americans ages 65 and older had used cannabis in the previous year. Among those people, 40.5% reported consuming cannabis through food or drinks. Meanwhile, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration found that 22.4% of American adults used cannabis in 2025.

Americans’ drinking habits are changing, too. A 2026 Gallup survey found that just 54% of U.S. adults consume alcohol, down from 62% in 2023. While the figures don't establish that people are replacing alcohol with cannabis, they reflect changing consumption habits. It seems people are increasingly opting out of Blackout Wednesday and opting into Green Wednesday.

The growing conversation around edibles also comes with an vital reminder: Cannabis-infused foods and drinks can take longer to produce noticeable effects than inhaled cannabis, and they should always be clearly labeled and kept away from children.

Between the sales numbers, viral cousin-walk jokes, and brands embracing the tradition, Green Wednesday is becoming a recognizable part of the Thanksgiving season. So when someone inevitably asks whether anyone wants to go for a walk after dinner, just know that an entire industry has been preparing for that moment.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

A classic grilled cheese is a thing of both beauty and comfort. And of course, a simple sandwich such as this is open to interpretation, with many putting their own spin on it, like making it Swiss-style with raclette cheese or switching up the grilling process by using an air fryer, like Ree Drummond. But there's an easy addition you can make to your next grilled cheese that will make it even tastier (and it's not mayo or butter, though you can certainly use either): It's store-bought caramelized onion dip.

When spread onto the bread and covered in cheese, then warmed through in a hot pan, caramelized onion dip brings a burst of flavor and a compelling texture to the sandwich. Of course, it's definitely savory, but the caramelized onions also introduce a subtly sweet element to grilled cheese, creating a flavor sensation that is much more interesting for your taste buds. Meanwhile, the dip melts into the cheese, adding to the creaminess, while the onions introduce a little toothsome variety to chew on, beyond the softness of the filling and the crispness of the bread.

Trader Joe's Caramelized Onion Dip is one great store-bought option, and it's part of the store's regular lineup, so you should be able to find it year-round (unless it has sold out). Whole Foods also sells a version under its 365 brand, which Amazon Prime members can shop for on Amazon.

In a recent development, if you have the desire to take things a step further, you might try a mix-in or two that can elevate the taste of the dip (and therefore, your entire sandwich). That might include some dried cranberries, which can help draw out the aforementioned sweetness of the onions, creating an even bolder contrast in your salty grilled cheese. You also might play to the richness and crumble up some crisp bacon into the base. Or enhance the savory, aromatic vibes by adding both thinly sliced scallions and chives.

In a recent development, now, if you're having trouble finding caramelized onion dip at your grocery store, you could always make your own, though cooking down the onions properly can be laborious. If standing over your stove for 45 minutes doesn't appeal to you, Ina Garten cuts down on the time by using a larger pot, which allows the onions to cook more evenly and efficiently. But if you'd rather skip the cooking altogether, you might find the adjacent caramelized onion jam on store shelves. This won't be as creamy as the dip, but it will still impart that same rich, savory, and slightly sweet flavor, so it's a decent substitution.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

In a recent development, pot roast is one of those simple homemade meals that may take a long time to cook but is pretty hands-off in the Crock Pot. Just brown the meat, add your ingredients, and let the cooker do its job. There are plenty of ways to upgrade a basic pot roast and some interesting regional pot roast dishes, and this simple trick is a bit of both. To give your pot roast a hint of Southern twang, add a packet of dry ranch seasoning. Similar to a set-it-and-forget-it easy French dip sandwich but Southern, a bit of ranch in your pot roast will give you some delightfully intense flavor and get you darn near a classic Mississippi pot roast.

In a recent development, ranch seasoning is basically an off-the-shelf, ready-to-go spice packet containing multiple seasonings — usually salt, onion powder, garlic powder, and other dried herbs and spices, like parsley and black pepper. Most brands also contain buttermilk and whey, which will add a bit of a creaminess factor, but you don't have to worry about the roast tasting like a bottle of ranch dressing because the mix will cook down with added beef stock and natural juices to form a nice, thick gravy. It will come out rich, bold, and savory with just a hint of tanginess from the buttermilk. Once your roast is nice and tender, you can simply slice it (or shred it) up and serve it Italian-beef or French-dip style, preferably with some melted cheese on top. The first bite through the bread into the perfectly tender and umami-rich, seasoned beef will make you a believer.

Sources indicate that if you want to go for a more or less standard pot roast route, you can simply rub your roast with a packet of Hidden Valley Ranch Seasoning, available online and in stores, or something similar, and cook it how you normally would with beef stock, potatoes, onions, carrots, and whatever other veg you like to use. To go full-on Mississippi roast, you can forgo the veggies and slow cook it with the ranch coating, beef stock or au jus gravy mix, and a half dozen or more whole pepperoncini. Up the spice level with extra hot peppers or use the whole jar. You can even add a bit of the brine for some supplementary heat, plus a zingy kick of vinegar. This will get you closer to an actual Mississippi pot roast, which typically features noted peppers.

For the bread, something that will hold up to the moisture of the roast is ideal. Toasted French bread adds a crunchy texture, but a toasted hoagie roll works great, and a thick sourdough will add a little extra tang. You'll want a cheese that melts easily, so you can quickly broil it without overcooking the bread. A simple mozzarella is an easy, mild choice, but a nice Gruyère will bring a richer and nuttier flavor with some subtle sweetness.

Ranch-seasoned pot roast or the full Mississippi mix is also great on egg noodles, mashed potatoes, or rice, or you can make a simple open-faced sando with a thick Texas toast. For an even saltier, more savory roast, you can try a three-packet blend with ranch, brown gravy, and Italian-style salad dressing mixes. However, to get that good Southern flavor, don't veer too far off the ranch.

#498. Latest Update: 8 Trader Joe's Cheeses To Try And 4 To Skip

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2438 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic

Latest Update: 8 Trader Joe's Cheeses To Try And 4 To Skip

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2438 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there's nothing like going to Trader Joe's before hosting a party and stocking up on cool and unusual cheeses.
  • None of the cheeses I tried were bad, some just weren't worth it for one reason or another, at a time when we're all watching our budgets extra closely.
  • It has been revealed that cranberry Chèvre Goat Cheese is not the only fruit studded fresh goat cheese at Trader Joe's, but it was the first one the store introduced, and it persists for good reason!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there's nothing like going to Trader Joe's before hosting a party and stocking up on cool and unusual cheeses. It's the perfect time to try something new or introduce your loved ones to one of your long-standing favorites. Trader Joe's has dozens of cheese at any given time and it can be a little intimidating to narrow down the options. To help out, I sampled some Trader Joe's cheeses to determine which you absolutely need to try, and which you're safe to skip.

None of the cheeses I tried were bad, some just weren't worth it for one reason or another, at a time when we're all watching our budgets extra closely. As touted in Trader Joe's incredibly easy return policy, every single product has been tried (and loved) by a firm representative, so the chances of ending up with something that's objectively bad are pretty slim. Still, there were eight truly standout cheeses among my sampling, and four that you can take a pass on. Prices may vary based on your location.

It has been revealed that cranberry Chèvre Goat Cheese is not the only fruit studded fresh goat cheese at Trader Joe's, but it was the first one the store introduced, and it persists for good reason! Despite its simple composition (a log of fresh goat cheese rolled in sweetened dried cranberries), it is surprisingly complex. It's creamy, tart, and sweet all at once, and the chewy cranberry pieces keep it texturally interesting. It adds a freshness that can help cut through the other heavy, rich options on your cheeseboard, and it's also super versatile.

If cranberry sauce isn't your preferred vessel for the fruit at the holidays, use this cheese in place of Trader Joe's equally delicious blueberry vanilla goat cheese to make a two-ingredient appetizer with puff pastry sheets. Or, serve the Cranberry Chèvre Goat Cheese with dinner and let your guests slather it on their rolls, instead. Perhaps the most inspired option is using the seasonally perfect fresh goat cheese as a spread for your Thanksgiving leftovers sandwich to take it to a whole new level.

Trader Joe's Comté Cheese is the kind of cheese you could expect to find at specialty cheese shop, and probably for a lot more money. That is, in part, because all Comté cheese is subject to Appellation d'Origine Protégée (AOP), which are rules that dictate how and where it is made.

In a recent development, the AOP stamp on Trader Joe's Comté is how you know it's the real deal and follows those same regulations. It's made in just one Alpine region of France (in one of about 134 small villages) using raw milk from one of only two specific breeds of cow, and it is aged for at least four months. The result is a Comté that is firm but creamy, with a somewhat intense smell and a delicately funky flavor. It's definitely one to try, but serve it at room temperature as intended to experience the unique aroma and taste of this strictly-regulated cheese.

Whether or not you have specifically heard of Emmentaler (also called Emmental) cheese, chances are pretty good that you have eaten it. It is the quintessential Swiss cheese that most Americans think of when they hear the term, though there are actually several Swiss cheese varieties.

Industry observers note that trader Joe's Emmentaler has a mild, somewhat sweet and nutty flavor that would be delicious on a ham and Swiss sandwich with Dijon mustard. Emmentaler is even the ultimate fondue cheese. So why is it a skip this time? It does not offer much to set it apart from a Swiss cheese you could buy at any other grocery store. Instead, spend your hard earned money on one of the other kinds of cheese that you can only find exclusively at Trader Joe's. Because, trust us, there are a lot of unique kinds to try at TJ's you can't get anywhere else.

Despite the fact that this Trader Joe's cheese is literally called Unexpected Cheddar Cheese, I'd never tried it, thinking it was just like any other aged cheddar I could buy. I was very wrong (and have since learned my lesson on believing TJ's packaging). There's a reason this cheese came in at No. 2 on our Trader Joe's Product Hall of Fame ranking, and if you've never tried it, now's really the time.

In a recent development, this cheddar has a really nice nuttiness along with its sharp flavor. It is harder and a bit crumblier than many cheddar cheeses, and has those distinctive crunchy crystals typically found more often in varieties like aged Parmigiano-Reggiano. Those crystals are formed during the aging of certain kinds of cheeses, especially in Italy, and are part of what makes Trader Joe's Unexpected Cheddar so delectable. The crumbly texture might not make it the best cheese for slicing up for sandwiches, but you'll enjoy it a hundred different other ways before it even occurs to you to care about that.

Recent findings suggest that trader Joe's Cheddar Cheese with Caramelized Onions has been my go-to cheese purchase for over a decade, and, all these years later, it still stands up. It has a softer texture than the store's Unexpected Cheddar, so it slices and melts it a bit more easily, but the caramelized onion flavor is where this cheese really shines. There's nothing else like it.

It has been revealed that it isn't just onions and cheese, either. The flavor is accomplished by blending a caramelized onion marmalade with an English cheddar cheese. The marmalade has a depth of flavor thanks to cider vinegar, red currant juice, lemon juice, olive oil, clove, cinnamon, and ginger. The warm sweetness of the caramelized onion marmalade is expertly balanced with the salty umami flavor of the cheddar itself, and the little bits of onion throughout make it visually and texturally interesting. This is the ideal cheese to bring to a book club meeting (trust me) and goes well with virtually everything.

The double bottles of bubbly being popped open on the front of this cheese's packaging had me hoping for something celebration worthy, but Trader Joe's English Cheddar Cheese with Champagne just isn't it. It's a perfectly fine cheddar cheese, if a bit on the extra salty side, but I had to really concentrate to pick up on any flavor notes that indicated the presence of Champagne.

According to the ingredients, this cheese includes actual Champagne, as well as Marc de Champagne brandy, which is made by distilling all the parts of the grapes that are leftover after being pressed for Champagne. Still, I had to really search for anything I might call Champagne flavor, which was a letdown. At the end of the day, it just wasn't as delicious as the Unexpected Cheddar or the variety with caramelized onions, despite being the most expensive of the bunch at $12.99 per pound.

Sources indicate that I don't think I've ever had a bad Brie, but I can confidently say that I've never had a Brie more delicious than Trader Joe's Triple Cream Brie with Wild Mushrooms. Admittedly, I'm a massive fan of mushrooms already, but I'm so used to having Brie with jammy fruits that it never occurred to me that the cheese would really shine when paired with the earthy flavors of wild mushrooms.

Served at room temperature with crackers or crusty bread, it spreads like a dream and needs absolutely nothing to improve it. That noted, there's nothing like a baked Brie to make a gathering feel like a party and this wild mushroom variety is no exception. If you're short on time, use your microwave to make a "baked" Brie. You'll still get the delicious, gooey texture everyone loves in baked Brie.

Something I didn't learn until I was in my late 20s is that not everyone eats the rind on Brie, despite the fact that it's completely edible (and delicious). If you're not a fan of the earthy rind, you're probably not going to be a fan of the earthy mushrooms in this cheese, either, but I hope you'll give it a chance.

Recent findings suggest that trader Joe's Huntsman Cheese looks very different from other options in the cheese case, with its defined white and orange striped layers. Those different stripes are actually two iconic British cheeses: double Gloucester and Blue Stilton.

The two cheeses work together beautifully. The double Gloucester has a smooth flavor with a somewhat firm texture, while the Blue Stilton, which has a Protected Designation of Origin, is sharp and a bit more crumbly (though it's also creamy at room temperature). While the streaks in the Blue Stilton are indeed mold, it's totally scientifically safe to eat the mold in blue cheese.

Recent findings suggest that what I love most about this cheese, other than its very unique appearance that makes it perfect for entertaining, is that its a great introduction to blue cheese for people who are leery of its strong flavor. By pairing the Blue Stilton with the double Gloucester, the flavors are well-balanced while still being complex and delicious. Lure your guests in with the striking appearance and amazing flavor of the Huntsman Cheese, then hit them with the Grand Blue (more on that beauty shortly).

I really wanted to love Trader Joe's Pink Peppercorn Fontina Cheese. It's very eye-catching with its vibrant pink coating and I'd incorrectly assumed that pink peppercorns meant it would be a spicy addition to my cheese selection. Avoid making the same mistake I did and take a minute to learn all about the different kinds of peppercorns, including the fact that pink peppercorns aren't true peppercorns and are more closely related to cashews than black peppercorns.

According to recent reports, still, the company's description of the cheese suggests a level of spice that just wasn't there. Instead, the cheese had an almost sweet vegetal flavor. A closer inspection of the ingredients revealed that the peppercorn seasoning blend also includes freeze dried strawberries, strawberry powder, and dehydrated red bell pepper, which made sense in hindsight. The flavors ended up tasting a bit muddled, though the cheese has some promise if it were paired with the right cracker, fruit, or other accompaniment. While it's certainly pretty, it's not worth the effort to make it truly exceptional.

One of the great things about being someone who is unabashedly a fan of blue cheese is that I never feel bad taking a decent sized serving from a cheese platter at an event. Pair it with a crunchy cracker and some red grapes, and I'm in heaven. But even I didn't know that blue cheese could be as good as Trader Joe's Grand Blue Cheese.

It has been revealed that this blue cheese is unbelievably creamy. I would have been hard pressed to crumble it unless it was straight from a very cold refrigerator. At room temperature, it sliced almost like soft butter and spread easily on crackers and bread. This is the blue cheese to serve with a black and blue burger, with the cheese melted on top of the patty, or on a pizza with figs, prosciutto, and a balsamic reduction. It's so creamy that I'd love to try it mixed into mac and cheese, if I can manage to make it last long enough next time I buy it (but the need to eat it straight-up might win out).

Havarti is a creamy Danish cheese that holds up super well to both slicing and melting, which makes it a great addition to recipes and on your cheese board. It has a relatively mild, somewhat sweet flavor that lends well to the addition of herbs, peppers, and spices. Perhaps the most iconic variety is Havarti with dill, and Trader Joe's version is worth adding to your shopping list.

Recent findings suggest that fresh dill is used in a lot of Nordic and Scandinavian cooking, so it makes sense that it's a perfect companion to a Danish cheese like Havarti. Trader Joe's Havarti with dill is absolutely packed with the bright herb. If you're the type of person who loves anything dill pickle flavored, you're going to love this cheese. Add it to anything that could use an herbaceous boost, but I highly recommend pairing it with Trader Joe's Unexpected Cheddar for a grilled cheese sandwich that's out of this world. For a bright crunch that brings out the cheese's sweetness, add some crisp apple slices, too. Thank me later.

Prior to trying Trader Joe's Toscano Cheese Dusted With Cinnamon, I'd never actually heard of Toscano cheese. It turns out that that's because it's based on another cheese entirely, with a few vital differences. Interestingly enough, while the retailer carries other cheeses with protected status, its Toscano is an interpretation rather than a faithful rendering of Italian Pecorino Toscano, which has a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO).

Italian Pecorino Toscano is a sheep's milk cheese made primarily in Tuscany, while Trader Joe's Toscano (both this cinnamon dusted version and other varieties it offers) are made from cow's milk in Wisconsin. There's nothing inherently wrong with either of those characteristics, and the cinnamon dusting on the cheese gives it a pleasantly warm sweetness, but it feels a bit like a bait and switch. The retailer describes the cheese as being like cheddar in texture and Parmesan in flavor, but I found that it was kind of bland compared to other options, and not even the dusting of cinnamon made it worth the buy.

Sources indicate that to ensure a wide range of Trader Joe's cheese, I gathered varieties from all around the world and across many cheese-making styles. While I would happily sample every variety Trader Joe's has to offer, I stuck to a budget of $75, which still allowed me to splurge on a few options and sample a total of 12 cheeses.

It has been revealed that each cheese was tried  first on its own to allow its natural flavor profile a chance to shine. Initial impressions were gathered based on how much I enjoyed the cheese, how much of it I wanted to keep eating, and whether it felt worth it for the cost. That last criterion included considerations like whether the cheese was memorable and how excited I would be to introduce it to a friend. The following day, I prepared a cheese board with all of the cheese samples, two types of crackers, and warm toasted baguette, which I enjoyed with my husband while watching television to solidify my recommendations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Recent findings suggest that when you're a fan of eggs, they can be pretty delicious however it is that they come off the stove or out of the oven. Even so, sometimes you're in the mood for something that doesn't require a lot of preparation yet is adaptable and tastes delicious. That's where scrambled eggs come in. They have a beautiful texture — whether you like them super soft and slightly gooey or a bit on the crispy side. There are a lot of different techniques, and some ways to cook them are better than others – like cooking them in water is probably a bad idea. Following some expert tips for scrambled eggs can get you to full-on restaurant quality; for example, fresh eggs at room temperature will give you great-tasting results that cook evenly. But when you want to keep it super simple at home, you can improve your everyday scrambled eggs by adding in a little bouillon.

Sources indicate that either beef or chicken bouillon will work. Beef bouillon will give your eggs a deep, unctuous taste that can be delicious, but may be a bit heavy if you're not looking for something super bold. Using a little chicken bouillon, on the other hand, will add some bright, salty notes that still have plenty of extra umami. Chicken bouillon will bring out the natural savory, even slightly sweet flavor of the eggs without overpowering them — which makes sense because they're both, well, chicken. Whichever you choose to use, bouillon makes a super easy addition to your scrambled eggs that really only takes a few extra seconds of work.

It has been revealed that as far as the bouillon goes, really anything will work — although it is often easier to get exact smaller measurements with powdered jars or pastes, like Better Than Bouillon Premium Roasted Chicken Base. Most standard bouillon cubes are equal to 1 teaspoon of bouillon powder or paste, but it can differ between brands, so take a look at the label. You'll want about a quarter teaspoon per three eggs. You can simply whisk the bouillon into the raw eggs with whatever seasonings and dairy you'd normally use (although you may want to lay off extra sodium because it's already quite salty), then scramble them to your preference. You can even wait to add the bouillon until the eggs have begun to set, then remove them from the heat and fold in the bouillon, so it just sort of melts in.

According to recent reports, if you want to go beyond milk or cream, you can try it with a little crème fraîche, sour cream, or cream cheese, or even a Gruyère or sharp cheddar. Pepper is a must to bring out your egg's full potential, and you might want to even try a pinch of sugar for a hit of sweetness that blends in nicely — especially with chicken bouillon. As for the veggies and herbs, this trick will go great with pretty much everything you usually like to see in your eggs; just consider the flavor profile if you're using beef versus chicken. You can even use canned veggies in your scramble; for example, canned tomatoes are subtly sweet and tangy, pairing excellently with chicken bouillon while canned mushrooms add umami and even more depth to beef.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as one of America's favorite fast food items, burgers are something you've almost certainly ordered from a chain at least once in your life — but not all chains are created equal. Everyone has a favorite, so the question of which is best is bound to stir up some fiery debate. Even so, we didn't let that stop us from ranking nine of America's favorite burger chains, and coming out on top of our list was Culver's.

Founded in Sauk City, Wisconsin, Culver's now has more than 1,000 locations across more than two dozen U.S. states. Its flagship item, the ButterBurger, is served on a fluffy Kaiser bun, and customers have the option to customize it with a long list of toppings, including some world-class Wisconsin cheese slices. Living up to its founding state's nickname as America's Dairyland, Culver's treats dairy as a core part of the menu. Its famous Wisconsin Cheese Curds arrive breaded and gooey, while its fresh frozen custard is the perfect way to round off a meal.

Industry observers note that culver's uses fresh, never-frozen beef, with its cooked-to-order patties made from a flavorful blend of sirloin, chuck, and plate. But what really sets it apart from chains like Shake Shack and Five Guys is the seasoning. Culver's uses salt and pepper, while Five Guys forgoes seasoning altogether. The chain argues its beef is so good that seasoning is unnecessary, but not all customers buy that reasoning.

Meanwhile, Shake Shack does season its patties, but Culver's has one not-so-secret ingredient that tips the scales in its favor: butter. It's spread on the crown of the bun, which is then toasted until golden, adding a rich flavor that makes the bun just as tasty as the patty.

Sources indicate that while the taste and quality of food certainly play a major role in where we rank a chain, they aren't the only factors to consider. On Reddit, one customer shared why they love Culver's: "[It's] probably the best [all-around] fast food there is," they claimed. "[High-quality] ingredients, consistent, always hot[,] and the restaurants are always clean." Which brings us to one seriously underappreciated category: cleanliness.

Just think about it: A good meal can rapidly be soured by a grimy dining area. Fast food often gets a bad rap for the quality of its food, but when it comes to hygiene, the best chains can easily hold their own against high-end sit-down restaurants. Culver's is no exception, and customers and media outlets have even credited it with having some of the cleanest bathrooms in the fast food game, which can only be a good thing.

Beyond cleanliness, Culver's is also one of the few major fast food chains left that's still family-owned. Rather than answering to shareholders, the company still has co-founder Craig Culver as its chairman. This has seen Culver's put plenty back into its community, most notably through its Thank You Farmers Project; the chain's website states that it has helped raise more than $8 million for agricultural education since 2013. Much of that comes from Scoops of Thanks Day, when customers get a scoop of custard in exchange for a $1 donation to their local Future Farmers of America chapter.

#495. 8 Fish With More Protein Than Salmon

8 Fish With More Protein Than Salmon

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that unless you've been living under a rock, you'll know that protein-maxxing is all the rage right now.
  • Salmon may be the most popular high-protein fish, and 100 grams of the farmed Atlantic variety contains around 20.3 grams of protein.
  • Sources indicate that tuna sits at or near the very top of the seafood protein hierarchy thanks to its lean, muscular build, but beyond whole fish, another serious source of protein is the canned variety.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that unless you've been living under a rock, you'll know that protein-maxxing is all the rage right now. The conversation largely revolves around go-to options like chicken breast, but we'll let you in on a little-known secret: Several meats out there actually outrank poultry when it comes to the macronutrient. Among them are certain types of fish, a protein source that often gets sidelined in the conversation, but leaving it out would be a serious mistake. Aside from being delicious, versatile, and (much of the time) budget-friendly, fish is also seriously easy to cook.

Salmon may be the most popular high-protein fish, and 100 grams of the farmed Atlantic variety contains around 20.3 grams of protein. That's already impressive, since it beats the 18.2 grams found in the same amount of 90% lean ground beef and comes up just under 2 grams shy of chicken breast. Compared to other fish, however, salmon actually gets outdone.

Sources indicate that tuna sits at or near the very top of the seafood protein hierarchy thanks to its lean, muscular build, but beyond whole fish, another serious source of protein is the canned variety. At face value, a tiny, oily anchovy isn't much to look at. But once these fish are packed tightly into cans, you're left with a surprisingly concentrated source of protein, along with a healthy dose of other beneficial nutrients. If anchovies pack too much of a punch for your taste, canned sardines also make for an excellent high-protein swap — and that's only the beginning.

Salty, briny, and often budget-friendly, canned anchovies contain a whopping 25.4 grams per 100-gram serving. You can enjoy them straight from the can since they're already cured, or if you want to take a more elevated approach, take a cue from the Portuguese and use them as an elegant garnish on toast alongside capers, good-quality olive oil, pickled red onions, and a sprinkling of parsley for good measure.

Recent findings suggest that sardines might be tiny, but they're loaded with protein (around 24 grams per 100 grams, to be precise). Like anchovies, they're an oily, nutrient-rich fish, but they set themselves apart with a milder, less salty flavor. Often sold whole, they make for a visually appealing garnish if you're looking to add a little drama to your dishes, and since canned sardines have already been cooked, they're good to eat straight out of the tin.

Yellowfin tuna, also known as ahi, is one of the more premium tuna species out there. Alongside its firm, beef-like texture and clean flavor, it's loaded with protein, with a 100-gram serving containing around 24.7 grams. It's also exceptionally versatile, since suppliers cut it into loins, saku blocks, and steaks for a hearty meal, while thinly sliced or cubed pieces work wonders in a tropical poke bowl or as delicious nigiri if you're craving something lighter.

According to recent reports, bluefin is the undisputed king of tuna; it's prized for sushi and sashimi, and its price can reach heights that can only be described as absurd — a 612-pound bluefin once sold for $3 million at a 2019 Tokyo auction. Like its price, its protein content sits on the higher end of the spectrum, too, reaching roughly 23 grams per 100-gram serving. But bluefin is better known for its impressive fat content, with the fatty otoro belly especially prized for its smooth, buttery texture.

Industry observers note that tilapia is one of the most popular fish in America, and despite its bargain price tag, it delivers a serious amount of protein, with a 100-gram serving containing 26.2 grams. It's also a solid pick if you've got sustainability in mind, since responsibly farmed tilapia can be relatively easy on the environment. This lean whitefish has a firm, flaky texture and mild flavor that stands up beautifully to grilling or pan-searing, making for a quick and satisfying weeknight dinner.

Recent findings suggest that halibut is a fan favorite that just edges out salmon's protein content, with approximately 20.8 grams per 100 grams. Despite those similar protein profiles, halibut is a lower-fat alternative with a considerably less fishy taste, making it a popular pick for those who have yet to come around on salmon. There are plenty of ways to prepare it, and grilling, pan-frying, or baking will all make for a delicious meal.

Notable for its vibrant red skin, firm white flesh, and uniquely sweet, nutty flavor, red snapper is a hugely popular seafood choice that packs 20.51 grams of protein per 100-gram serving. Compared to your everyday whitefish, its price tag ranges from moderate to expensive, but it more than makes up for it with a wonderfully tender texture. To make use of its dramatic red hue, pair your snapper with seasonings and aromatics and bake it whole.

Sources indicate that if you've grown tired of salmon's ever-rising price tag, look no further than rainbow trout. Also available as steelhead trout, this seriously underrated fish has a milder, more delicate flavor than salmon and leaner, finer-flaked flesh. Rainbow trout contains 20.5 grams of protein per 100-gram serving, though its leaner profile makes it less forgiving than salmon at very high heat, so it's best suited to gentler methods like pan-frying or whole roasting.

People love soy sauce for a next-level steak marinade not just because of its salt, but also its complexity. If, however, you want to eschew the sodium and bump up that deliciously fermented flavor, you need koji, a type of rice critical to Japanese sake production.

Recent findings suggest that when you inoculate short-grain rice with Aspergillus oryzae mold, it slowly breaks down proteins and carbohydrates into an ingredient you can then ferment for sake or dry for use as a savory, shelf-stable ingredient. This is koji, a lesser-known source of umami that is nonetheless a potent marinade ingredient. While the differences are more subtle than with soy sauce, it gives you great control over your meat's final flavor profile and leaves you room to add other seasonings, like the best salts for seasoning steak, herbs, and spices.

If you use shio koji, a type of marinade made by combining koji rice with salt and water, you can even tenderize your meat. The sodium helps the beef retain moisture, while the enzymes break down proteins, leaving your steak tender and flavorful no matter how you prepare it. Just be careful, as some varieties have added sugars that can unexpectedly sweeten your meat too much. While they won't exactly candy your steak, they might overhaul your food's taste.

Industry observers note that whether you use wet shio koji or dry, shelf-stable koji, this ingredient is extremely useful and easy to add to marinades. Just keep in mind that its enzymes remain active when wet, so you'll want to be careful about how long you let your steak sit before cooking.

Industry observers note that dry, shelf-stable koji is quite versatile but may require extra steps. Grinding it into a powder and adding a few tablespoons to your marinade is a great way to boost umami. However, you can also create a dry crust on your steak and let it sit in your fridge for a couple of days. This can mimic some of the effects of long dry-aging, helping your beef develop an impressive level of complexity in only 48 hours. However, you'll want to rinse the rice off your meat and pat it dry before cooking, as its starches and natural sugars burn quite easily.

Shio koji is a bit easier to use and so delicious that you don't even need other marinade ingredients. Since it's able to thoroughly coat the meat, this is a great choice if you're working with tough cuts, like flank steak, that need some extra tenderizing. Two tablespoons per pound of protein should be plenty to get tender meat. To get a good crust, you'll still want to wipe off the excess rice and moisture and watch your heat, but it's an otherwise hands-off recipe that can taste like you spent hours fretting over the perfect marinade.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, rich, tender, and intensely flavorful, a well-prepared lamb chop is always guaranteed to be a crowd-pleaser. Compared to chicken, pork, and even most beef, lamb doesn't come cheap. And sitting at the top of the hierarchy are lamb chops. However, a delicious lamb meal doesn't always have to break the bank. One cut that's cheaper yet packs far more flavor is the seriously underrated lamb shoulder.

Recent findings suggest that much like most premium cuts of beef, lamb chops come from an extremely small, sought-after section of the animal. A single lamb yields only around eight to 10 desirable rib and loin chops, making them a limited commodity. Already, without texture and flavor considered, lamb chops already rein in a high price tag. Tenderness certainly plays a part in their appeal, too. Lamb is typically harvested before the animal reaches 12 months of age, meaning its muscle fibers are finer and more tender than those of mature sheep or cattle, and chops happen to be among the most tender cuts available. Pair that natural tenderness with their limited yield, and you've got a cut that commands a premium.

However, a higher price doesn't always equate to a more flavorful cut. Lamb shoulder proves this. Unlike the scarce rib and loin, the shoulder is a larger, less sought-after cut that comes from a harder-working muscle. Naturally, it contains more connective tissue and is less tender, which helps explain its lower price. Don't mistake that for inferior quality. The shoulder happens to be a richly marbled cut, giving it a fuller, more robust flavor than the relatively lean chops. So if you're after that rich, slightly gamey taste of lamb, shoulder can be every bit as rewarding as chops, if not more so.

Because lamb chops, whether they're taken from the loin or ribs, are so naturally tender, they're exceptionally well-suited to quick-cooking techniques like pan-searing or grilling. This makes them worth the price if you want a quick, low-effort weeknight meal. You don't even need to worry about a marinade, either. High-quality, tender cuts like loin or rib chops already have a potent natural flavor that doesn't need to be boosted by a marinade. Even so, if you want to literally spice things up, put together a classic Indian-style tandoori marinade using a blend of yogurt, ginger-garlic paste, and traditional spices like garam masala, cumin, turmeric, and Kashmiri chili powder for a seriously elevated spin.

If you'd rather keep things simple, borrow a tip from the Barefoot Contessa and ask your butcher to french the lamb. Frenched lamb chops are simply lamb rib chops where the meat, fat, and connective tissue have been completely scraped and trimmed away from the end of the rib bone. The contrast between the pearly white bone and the beautifully browned meat provides the elegant wow-factor fitting for the price of chops.

In a recent development, cooking lamb shoulder is considerably less hands-on than chops, but you pay for convenience with time. Its connective tissue means it's simply not built for quick cooking methods. Instead, shoulder benefits from low-and-slow methods like slow-roasting or braising, which allows the tough collagen to break down into gelatin, thus creating melt-in-your-mouth meat. If you'd rather have quicker-cooking shoulder meat, lamb shoulder chops have you covered. Unlike whole shoulder, thinner shoulder chops can be pan-seared or grilled — though it's worth noting that braising remains a far better option when you're working with thicker ones since they still have more connective tissue than your standard rib or loin chops.

When preparing steak, cooks often focus on selecting the best cut, then preparing it with a specific method to an ideal doneness. Less emphasis is placed on the fat employed for the task — although what you pour into the pan also impacts both the flavor and texture of your meal. So skip standard pantry staples like butter and oil, and try a version with beef tallow instead.

So — what is beef tallow? It's essentially rendered beef fat, an ingredient that lends numerous advantages to steak night. Foremost is the ultra-savory profile: Tallow is made by slowly cooking down beef trimmings, resulting in a rich, meaty taste. This staple works as a flavor enhancer in addition to a cooking medium, complementing the deep, savory character of steak. And if you buy a higher-quality grass-fed variety, you may impart even more complexity, introducing earthy and grassy notes to your dining experience.

In parallel, beef tallow helps create a mouthwatering crust. The ingredient boasts a higher smoke point than butter and some other fats. So whether you're searing on high heat or finishing the steak in the oven, the fat can withstand high temperatures, enabling browning and Maillard reactions that create a terrific crust. That adds up to an elevated steak experience, all from swapping out the fat that goes into the pan.

Recent findings suggest that preparing a steak with beef tallow doesn't require any special accommodations. The fat is solid at room temperature and can be shelf-stable when properly stored, making it an easy pantry addition. You'll only need about a tablespoon per portion: Simply spoon the tallow into the skillet, where it'll melt and cover the cooking surface. It's a cooking medium that's especially effective on cast iron — whether a griddle or a pan — as it can also be used to season the cookware. You can also use tallow when grilling by coating both the cut itself and the grill grates with a thin layer of beef fat.

Recent findings suggest that any steak cut can be prepared in tallow; just note that it lends a rich flavor. So if you're making a mild-tasting filet mignon, for example, the addition could be overpowering. It's better to pair tallow with robust cuts like a ribeye, porterhouse, or New York strip, thereby producing an especially beef-forward meal. Otherwise, there's no need to worry about the details. Simply add a spoonful to your pan and sear away; this staple makes for a dependably delicious steak experience.

In a recent development, flour tortillas and dairy, like cheddar and Colby jack cheeses, are also significant parts of the Tex-Mex food culture, as are queso dips and customizable combinations of rice, beans, proteins, and cheeses in a personal-sized bowl. Many of the restaurants on this list do just that, and all of them have been highly rated by fans for taste, price, and overall value. So, the next time you're craving fajitas, quesadillas, and refried beans, feel free to give one of these chains a visit to fulfill that hunger.

Recent findings suggest that founded in 1991, Mi Cocina is a beloved local chain with just over 20 locations throughout Texas, but the eatery's reputation stretches far further. The upscale Tex-Mex restaurant is just as known for its cocktails, especially the swirled Mambo Taxi Margarita, as it is for the food, such as the fajitas. The upscale brand's dishes include nachos al carbon, poblano chicken enchiladas, and pork picoso tamales that are so flavorful, you definitely won't want to put ketchup on them.

Customers rate the restaurant highly on user review platforms, with diners on Yelp saying things like, "Always consistently excellent! My go-to is the brisket tacos and a Dilemma Margarita!" Other guests agree, saying they always enjoy the food when they visit the chain. That reliability is one reason people are so quick to recommend the establishment. Even those who are quite particular about their Tex-Mex fall in love with the place, and many say they'll be back after their first time dining here.

Don't make the mistake of confusing Taco Cabana with Taco Bell. Both chains sell tacos, but the smaller restaurant still has a homemade feel, unlike the larger, Tex-Mex fast food super-seller. That's probably because Taco Cabana still makes its from-scratch food from fresh ingredients every day. The differences in flavor and feel in the restaurant's dishes are easy to identify, especially in the handmade flour tortillas. That helps ensure you'll never have to worry about one of the most vital elements of a satisfying burrito. And the ones here come overstuffed and covered in optional cheese sauce.

Diners here develop a passion for the chain, or as one TikTok commenter declared, "Taco Cabana is my FAVORITE fast food place. It beats Taco Bell hands down." It's not hard to see why someone might feel that way. Fans enjoy the restaurant's large portions, noting that nachos come in a box large enough to be mistaken for a pizza.

It has been revealed that the meats get their share of the limelight too, with customers recommending items like the beef and chicken fajita nachos, and the customizable protein bowl. One of the brand's latest hit items is the bean and cheese pie, a handheld psuedo-empanada filled with refried beans and yellow cheeses.

Uncle Julio's is an eatery that has understood the importance of making every dish from scratch since it opened several decades ago, and that includes the flour tortillas. The freshly made flatbread definitely tastes better than store-bought ones, which is why people can buy them by the dozen. And that's just one of the things that's made with care here. Dishes like guacamole that's made tableside and large burritos have led this Texas-based chain to expand into more than 30 locations.

According to recent reports, people appreciate the restaurant's salsa, which holds a great middle-ground between mild and spicy, and praise the bacon-wrapped shrimp, which pairs juicy, seasoned seafood with crispy and chewy slices of pork. Others say they often have enough of their meal left to take some home, especially with dishes like the chicken and steak fajitas or the Tex-Mex combination dinner.

This Tex-Mex establishment also has a unique dessert – interactive chocolate piñatas. Guests are encouraged to play with their food when the hanging ball of decorated chocolate is brought to the table. A few short taps later and the dessert cracks open to spill strawberries, churros, and other fruits onto the tray. It's another delicious and memorable way Uncle Julio's has found to fuse cultures before ending the evening.

Recent findings suggest that like several of the chains on this list, Fuzzy's Taco Shop was founded in Texas. But this one has gone on to become one of the largest of the homegrown brands, with more than 100 locations in 14 states. That growth was spurred forward by customers who enjoy the restaurant's sizable portions, flavors, and consistency on dishes ranging from breakfast burritos, quesadillas, nachos, and customizable bowls.

In a recent development, first-time diners are impressed by the guacamole and overall experience of eating at Fuzzy's, and say they'll no doubt be returning soon. Others make it a point to visit the chain often, saying it's a great spot for birria tacos. In fact, one fan on Facebook called the dish "top notch," adding that the meal was perfectly made. Items like the grilled steak bowl and seasoned chips are so tasty they can even help people who normally eat at other Mexican-inspired places make the switch to Fuzzy's.

In a recent development, guests are warmly greeted every time they walk through the doors at Moe's Southwest Grill, a tradition the business started at the first location in 2000. Since then, the firm has grown rapidly, now operating almost 550 stores across the nation. The brand is known for innovative flavors and good quality, and customers praise the queso, overstuffed burritos, and customizable bowls, which many say are better than other national brands.

A TikTok user posted about their experience getting a nearly full bag of chips after ordering his mains, and that kind of generosity isn't rare at the chain. Another fan noted how stuffed the birria stack they ordered was, saying it was heavy to pick up, while a first-time diner was impressed by how large the bowl they ordered was.

Fans of Moe's have plenty of choices to customize their bowls and other meals with, but many find their favorite items and stick with them. That loyalty had one customer declaring a half-hour drive to the nearest store wasn't too far to go for the food, showing that not even a little distance can keep people away when a queso craving strikes. Or, as one Tripadvisor reviewer stated, "... food is splendid! All around just great establishment. We loved everything, especially the queso!!".

The name Qdoba Mexican Eats might catch your attention, but it's the chain's food that keeps it. So much so that in the almost 30 years the restaurant has been open, Qdoba fans have formed a rivalry with those who prefer Chipotle, which just so happens to have also been founded in Denver in the 1990s. But Colorado residents prefer the smaller chain, with customers citing the brand's freshness, taste, and generosity with the queso keeps other national brands from comparing.

The establishment is known for the variety of fillings it offers, including steak and chicken that's grilled in-house. In addition to burrito bowls, you can customize a bowl of layered nachos, too. And the quesadillas can have some crunch added with a cheesy exterior crust. One Facebook user was so impressed by the restaurant that they posted, "I've been 5 times, the food is always fresh and hot [...] I've tried their quesadillas and bowl and I'm absolutely blown away every time with the quality. 10/10!".

Tex-Mex chains are popular and plentiful on the restaurant landscape, so narrowing down this list to the brands fans can't stop raving about took a bit of time. First, the criteria for how we'd be defining what makes a chain the best and what made it Tex-Mex were decided.

If the restaurants had a focus on flour tortillas, yellow cheeses, and cumin, alongside dishes, like nachos, enchiladas, fajitas, and queso, it qualified as a Tex-Mex establishment.

The eateries had to have more than a dozen locations and good reviews for taste, value, and consistency across multiple sources. Those platforms included social media posts and comments, message boards, user review sites, and professional reviews. The final list was compiled after each chain's specific instances of customer satisfaction were tallied.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, semolina is a coarse, pale-yellow flour made by grinding the endosperm of durum wheat, one of the hardest species of wheat there is.
  • According to recent reports, just don't go overboard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A classic French toast recipe is one of those comforting dishes that can be whipped up in a matter of minutes. However, one common problem people run into is soggy bread rather than a crisp, beautifully caramelized exterior. Unfortunately, sogginess is something of an occupational hazard when you're soaking bread in liquid. To give your slices more of a chance to thrive, all you need to do is add a little semolina flour to your soaking mixture. Two tablespoons per cup and a half of liquid is just about all you need.

In a recent development, semolina is a coarse, pale-yellow flour made by grinding the endosperm of durum wheat, one of the hardest species of wheat there is. Compared to standard, powdery all-purpose flour, semolina is higher in protein and fiber, and its coarse grains are well-suited to soaking up moisture. In French toast, that can be the difference between a soggy exterior and a crispy one. A small amount turns a watery custard into a more structured batter that clings to the bread instead of letting it drink up all that liquid and fall apart before it even reaches the frying pan. Its subtle nuttiness also adds a whole new layer of complexity to the flavor of the French toast, and would pair wonderfully with some cosy nutmeg and cinnamon.

According to recent reports, just don't go overboard. Semolina is still flour, so balance is key. Add too little and the mixture stays watery; add too much, and you end up with something closer to a paste than a batter. We recommend starting with a small amount, around a tablespoon, then adjusting until you reach your desired consistency. Semolina flour takes time to absorb liquid, so once you've added it, let the custard sit for a minimum of 10 minutes before adding your bread. Once it's rested, it should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.

In a recent development, semolina is one way to give French toast a crispy, lightly browned exterior, but it's by no means the only one. If you're having a hard time finding it, you can always swap in regular flour. The texture is different, but flour also absorbs liquid and thickens the batter, so you get largely the same effect, just without the nutty flavor. You could even skip the flour altogether and stir a cornstarch slurry into the custard, which packs even more thickening power. Just remember, as with semolina, moderation is key when adding flour or cornstarch into the mix.

In a recent development, beyond thickening the custard, there are plenty of other handy tricks for shatteringly crispy French toast. To improve both its texture and flavor, give your bread a generous dusting of sugar after it comes out of the custard (before it hits the heat). Alton Brown might prefer honey over sugar in his French toast, but we'd argue that's a rare mistake. See, once sugar hits the heat, it starts to caramelize, melting into a crisp, brûléed crust and infusing the bread with a rich, toasty flavor. Keep the heat moderate, since caramelization can quickly turn to burning without proper care.

In a recent development, if you're not sold on the idea of messing around with the batter or adding extra ingredients, you can guarantee crispy French toast from the get-go by using stale bread. This might not sound too appetizing, but hear us out. Bread that's around one to two days old has lost a good chunk of its moisture, which leaves it firmer and drier. It acts like a sponge, soaking up the custard without turning to mush, so you get a rich, eggy center and a browned exterior instead of a soggy, limp slice.

Yet start trialing creative add-ins, and tuna salad welcomes a surprisingly wide array of ingredients. There are so many ways to take plain tuna salad to the next level. A sharp cheddar cheese is one unexpected flavor boost.

After all, creaminess is a central part of the dish's appeal. And as a dairy product, cheddar cheese offers such a smooth mouthfeel in spades. However, unlike a simple mayo dressing, the cheese comes with a punch. Aging develops complex flavors, which can vary from barely perceptible tartness to rich nuttiness to a bold bite. Usually, the older the cheddar, the more amplified the flavor — although as the cheese develops, it loses some creaminess to become crumbly.

So cube up the cheese, using two ounces per can of tuna, then stir everything up with some salt, onions, celery, and your other go-to tuna salad fold-ins. You'll get a dish that's still comforting, but also comes with revamped flair.

Originating by mistake, the tuna melt proves that fish and cheese do belong on the same plate, especially if tuna's involved.

Further embrace the two dishes by heating the cheddar cheese tuna salad. The cheese will turn molten inside — not only on top — of the fish, making for an extra-satisfying filling. Pair that with a nice bread, say a classic American white loaf, a deli-inspired rye, or a dependable sourdough, and you've got a terrific sandwich on your hands.

Not to say there's not more magic to explore with a cold cheddar tuna salad, too. The cheesy rendition is a befitting tuna pasta salad twist. Or balance out cheddar's richness by rolling the salad into lettuce wraps, a delicious appetizer option. Cheddar gives tuna salad that extra oomph, turning the basic dish into a centerpiece meal.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that this technique mimics a panini press, which functions by heating top and bottom metal plates connected by a hinge.
  • According to recent reports, the oven also has the advantage of providing ambient heat since it's an enclosed environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, whether you like it on its own or coupled with a bowl of roasted tomato soup, a grilled cheese is one of life's simple pleasures. Making one for yourself is simple enough in a pan or skillet. However, preparing half a dozen or more can be a pretty big undertaking on the stovetop. Fortunately, there's an easier way. By using a couple of baking sheets and your oven, you can conveniently whip up a large batch of these cheesy sandwiches that come out super crispy.

Sources indicate that this technique mimics a panini press, which functions by heating top and bottom metal plates connected by a hinge. This gets both sides of the sandwich crispy at the same time, eliminating the need for flipping. However, these presses have their downsides. The weight of the plates, for instance, can turn softer bread into a pancake. Baking sheets, on the other hand, are much lighter and won't compromise the integrity of more delicate breads.

According to recent reports, the oven also has the advantage of providing ambient heat since it's an enclosed environment. This means that your sandwich is getting heated on all sides instead of just the top and bottom, helping to create crisp crusts and melted cheese. However, you still need to preheat your top baking sheet for even crispness, since the bottom of your sandwiches could brown before the tops get crispy.

Sources indicate that depending on how many sandwiches you want to prepare, you can vary the size of the baking sheet you use. To make about six to eight at once, use a half-sheet pan, which measures about 18 inches by 13 inches and is probably the size you have at home. You can also use a quarter-sheet pan if you want to make fewer.

While the fat you spread on your bread (we recommend mayo for the crispiest results) will help ensure that your sandwiches don't stick to the baking sheets, you can also take a tip from Ina Garten and use parchment paper to line the pans for extra insurance. Also, don't stick to just using your baking sheets right side up. In fact, using your bottom pan upside down will allow for more airflow since the rim won't get in the way, thus crisping your sandwiches more effectively.

To make this technique really work, though, you're going to need to make sure you choose the right kind of cheese that will melt easily by the time the crusts of your sandwiches become golden brown. After all, you don't want to have to keep putting your grilled cheeses back in the oven to finish melting. The best options have a good balance of moisture and fat, and younger cheeses tend to be the go-to varieties that meet this standard. Some recommendations include Havarti, Gruyère, and cheddar. However, you can opt for some underrated (but tasty) cheeses to give your sandwiches extra character. You can also combine several types of cheese for a more varied flavor and texture.

  • The oil holds a Toscano Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) designation, which certifies that the extra virgin olive oil was produced in the region of Tuscany, Italy, according to specific standards.
  • According to recent reports, while the exact origin of the oil remains a mystery, what we do know for sure is that Tuscan olive oil sits among the best in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the best perks of a Costco membership is exclusive access to its wide range of bulk bargain buys. Its Italian section is among the most impressive, where you can purchase a 72-pound wheel of Parmigiano Reggiano or keep things simple with some dried pasta. But no matter what Italian delight you're cooking up, a good-quality olive oil is where the magic happens. To help curate the best meal possible, we ranked 11 of the best Italian foods you can buy at Costco, and its Kirkland Signature Toscano Extra Virgin Olive Oil landed itself a well-deserved spot.

The oil holds a Toscano Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) designation, which certifies that the extra virgin olive oil was produced in the region of Tuscany, Italy, according to specific standards. Like most Kirkland Signature grocery items, Costco contracts with outside producers rather than manufacturing the oil itself. Unfortunately, Costco keeps its suppliers under tight wraps, so it's difficult to pinpoint exactly where the oil comes from ... but there's nothing stopping us from guessing. Interestingly, oil from Tuscany's Montalbano subzone has been noted to have distinct notes of almond and artichoke, which also happens to be exactly how the taste of the oil is described on the back of the bottle.

According to recent reports, while the exact origin of the oil remains a mystery, what we do know for sure is that Tuscan olive oil sits among the best in the world. The region is home to numerous native cultivars, with three main ones making up the bulk of production. Another thing that sets Tuscan olive oil apart is its scarcity. The region only produces a tiny amount of oil compared to major producers like Calabria and Puglia, so consider it a privilege if you're able to get your hands on a Tuscan bottle.

Just by reading the label, you can tell this is an olive oil worth picking up. Extra virgin means the oil was extracted mechanically, without chemical solvents or excessive heat. Olives are crushed into a paste, then processed to separate the oil from the water and solids, all at low temperatures (cold extraction, in other words). Keeping things cool matters because excessive heat can strip away the delicate flavors and aromas that give good olive oil those fruity and peppery notes. That's a sharp contrast to regular olive oil, which is typically a blend of refined oil and a small amount of virgin oil. The refining process uses heat and other treatments to clean up lower-quality oil, leaving something milder and a lot less interesting.

Extra virgin olive oil isn't just the more artisanal option; it's often the more nutritious one, too. Unlike refined olive oils, it retains higher levels of polyphenols and other antioxidants, which may help fight oxidative stress and reduce chronic inflammation. Add in its starring role in the Mediterranean diet, which is widely studied for its long-term health benefits, and it's easy to see why nutritionists love the stuff. It's worth noting, however, that extra virgin olive oil generally has a lower smoke point than refined olive oil, which makes it particularly well-suited to dressings and light sauteing, though it can also be used for many higher-heat cooking applications.

Crostata Di Mele (Italian Apple Pie) Recipe

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, while working as a young pastry chef in an Italian trattoria, I had the great fortune of spending 3 weeks eating my way through Italy in an attempt to discover the most unique and tempting desserts each region had to offer.
  • In a recent development, my recipe for crostata di Mele (Italian apple pie) is a bakery-worthy homage to those delightful desserts, and it became a seasonal fixture on my pastry menu.
  • In a recent development, learning how to make the dough and filling for this crostata will give you a solid foundation for making other Italian pastries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, while working as a young pastry chef in an Italian trattoria, I had the great fortune of spending 3 weeks eating my way through Italy in an attempt to discover the most unique and tempting desserts each region had to offer. Although I tasted complex and ethereal cakes, pastries, and frozen delights, I kept coming back to the simple fruit crostatas: buttery crusts molded into tart pans or baked free-form in rustic rounds, topped with glistening fruits and cakey or custardy fillings. These desserts tasted like perfection in their simplicity and purity of flavors.

In a recent development, my recipe for crostata di Mele (Italian apple pie) is a bakery-worthy homage to those delightful desserts, and it became a seasonal fixture on my pastry menu. A traditional pasta frolla (Italian short dough) crust is filled with a lemon and vanilla-scented creme patissiere (pastry cream custard) and topped with tart, crisp apples and crunchy turbinado sugar. The warm crostata is given a finishing glaze of melted apricot preserves, then chilled for serving.

In a recent development, learning how to make the dough and filling for this crostata will give you a solid foundation for making other Italian pastries. The dough is easy to work with, and the pastry cream is a versatile filling for other treats, such as profiteroles, layer cakes, or napoleons.

There are 3 main components in the crostata di mele: the crust, the custard filling, and the toppings. For the crust, you will need all-purpose flour, granulated sugar, sea salt, cold unsalted butter, a large egg plus 1 yolk, vanilla extract, and the zest of a large lemon. The difference between this crostata dough and regular apple pie dough is the addition of eggs, which makes the dough slightly less flaky but more pliable for rolling and shaping. For the pastry cream, you will need whole milk, a vanilla bean, more lemon zest, 4 yolks, granulated sugar, and cornstarch. You will split the vanilla bean lengthwise to release the tiny black seeds into the milk, and the cornstarch acts as a thickening agent. To top the crostata, I like using apples that are crisp and tart, but that also have a balance of sweetness. Honeycrisp, Pink Lady, and Granny Smith are perfect apple varieties for this recipe. You will toss your apple slices with fresh lemon juice to prevent browning before baking, and use some melted butter to secure a crunchy sprinkling of turbinado sugar. To give your baked crostata a shiny finish, you will need apricot preserves to melt down and strain.

Combine the flour, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer bowl.

Add the butter a few pieces at a time and mix until pea-sized clumps form.

Add the egg, yolk, lemon zest, and vanilla, and mix until a dough forms.

Shape the dough into a disk, wrap in plastic, and refrigerate it for at least 30 minutes.

While the dough is chilling, heat the milk, vanilla bean, and lemon zest strips in a medium saucepan until it barely starts to simmer.

Remove the pan from the heat, cover, and steep for 10 minutes.

Place a medium glass bowl on a damp kitchen towel or mat to prevent slipping.

Add the egg yolks, sugar, and cornstarch and whisk until thick and pale yellow.

Remove the vanilla bean and zest strips with a slotted spoon, then discard.

Gradually add the warm milk to the egg mixture, whisking constantly.

Transfer the mixture back to the saucepan and cook over low heat, stirring frequently until it comes to a boil. Turn the heat to low and whisk constantly for 1 minute.

Recent findings suggest that remove the pan from the heat, then scrape the filling into a heat-proof bowl and press a piece of plastic wrap to the surface. Chill for at least 2 hours.

In a large bowl, toss the apple slices with the lemon juice.

Roll out the chilled dough to a 12-inch circle on a floured surface.

Roll out the chilled dough to a 12-inch circle on a floured surface.

Press the dough into the pan and trim the excess flush with the edge of the pan.

Spread the cooled pastry cream evenly over the bottom of the pastry shell.

Arrange the slices in concentric overlapping circles over the pastry cream, starting from the outer edge and working inward.

Brush the apples with the melted butter and sprinkle on the turbinado sugar.

Bake the crostata di mele for about 50 minutes until the crust is golden brown and the apples are tender.

While the crostata is baking, heat the apricot jam with 1 tablespoon of water in a small saucepan until warm and liquid.

Strain the jam if any large pieces of fruit remain.

Remove the crostata from the oven and immediately brush on the apricot glaze.

Cool the crostata completely in the pan on a rack before removing from the pan.

Slice the crostata and serve at room temperature or chilled.

Our bakery-worthy crostata di Mele (Italian apple pie) is filled with a lemon and vanilla-scented creme patissiere and topped with tart, crisp apples.

Recent findings suggest that the crostata is one of the most continuously made dessert forms found in Italian baking, dating back to the 1400s. Not only is the crostata found in pastry shops and on restaurant menus, but it is also the one dessert that many people make at home with whatever ingredients are on hand. This kind of humble tart was likely consumed at breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

Recent findings suggest that the crostata di mele probably originated in northern Italy, where apples are grown in abundance. In order to highlight the fresh flavor of the apples, crostata de mele is spiced with a light hand. Subtle cinnamon and a hint of nutmeg might be used, along with the zest of a lemon, as in this recipe. With only a few simple ingredients, the recipe is also dependent on using a light hand in preparation. The dough should be minimally handled to prevent a tough or shrunken crust. The pastry cream must be carefully tempered to prevent lumps from forming. And nothing should get in the way of the apples being the star.

Even though there may seem to be a lot of steps to this recipe, there are lots of ways to do advance prep to save time. First, your crostata dough can be mixed, shaped into a disk, wrapped, and chilled for several days in the refrigerator. You can also freeze this dough for up to 3 months. Once you are ready to roll out the dough, allow it to come to cool to room temperature before you shape it. You can also roll out and fill your tart pan, then wrap the unbaked shell and refrigerate or freeze until it is time to fill and bake.

The pastry cream should only be made 1 or 2 days in advance, and this custardy filling should not be frozen unless it is layered into a dessert (too much separation will occur). Wait until just before baking to spread the pastry cream into your tart shell so that the dough will not become soggy.

From experience, I know that this crostata di mele will stay fresh, tasty, and sliceable for almost a week under refrigeration. That said, it is crucial to always keep the crostata chilled to prevent bacterial growth in the custard layer. Typically, 3-5 days is the best range for serving this dessert.
